item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Real-world use of digital therapeutics for substance use disorders in primary care: Observational study of the engagement cascade by substance type
item.description:
Background: Patient engagement with digital therapeutics for substance use disorder (SUD) in primary care remains poorly understood. We analyzed engagement in routine care and whether specific types of substance use are associated with greater engagement.

Methods: This real-world observational study analyzed 83 primary care patients prescribed reSET® or reSET-O®, US Food and Drug Administration-authorized digital therapeutics for SUD. Substance types (unhealthy alcohol, cannabis, and other drug use) were identified from routine health screens and clinical diagnoses. The primary outcome was progression through four engagement cascade milestones: app activation, user guide completion, completion of ≥ one module, and treatment completion. Vendor logfiles provided weekly module counts. Logistic regression evaluated associations between substance use and engagement, adjusting for age and sex.

Results: Overall, 50.6% of patients activated the app, 45.8% completed the guide, 38.6% completed ≥ one module, and 13.3% met the vendor-defined treatment completion criterion. Among those who activated it, the median number of modules completed was 4 (interquartile range 1-32); half of module users stopped by week 4. Unhealthy alcohol use was associated with higher odds of app activation, user guide completion, and completion of ≥ one module (adjusted odds ratios [95% confidence intervals] = 2.84 [1.10-7.66], 3.48 [1.32-9.82], and 3.67 [1.32-11.26], respectively). Cannabis and other drug use were not associated with engagement milestones.

Conclusions: Engagement with prescription-based digital therapeutics in primary care varies by substance type and is concentrated in the first month of use. Overall, engagement remains limited. Future research should validate these findings and refine engagement strategies.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Medication for opioid use disorder following urine drug testing: An observational cohort study of linked national laboratory and medical and pharmacy claims data
item.description:
Background and aims: Urine drug testing (UDT) is commonly used in opioid use disorder (OUD) care to assess substance use and inform clinical decision-making, yet little is known about how opioid UDT results are associated with subsequent medication for opioid (MOUD) use and adherence. This study examines the association between opioid UDT, post-UDT MOUD use, and treatment adherence using linked national laboratory and medical and pharmacy claims data.

Design: Retrospective quantitative observational cohort study.

Setting: United States, using linked national laboratory and adjudicated medical and pharmacy claims data covering all 50 states and Washington DC.

Participants: Adults aged 18-64 years with at least one opioid UDT between June 2017 and May 2025 and continuous medical and pharmacy enrollment for 180 days prior and 365 days following the initial test (N = 759,153).

Measurement: Primary outcomes were post-UDT MOUD use within 365 days after opioid UDT and MOUD adherence. Treatment adherence was defined using claims-based gaps consistent with prior literature. Multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for demographics, insurance type, comorbid mental and physical health conditions, prior MOUD use, and state-level fixed effects.

Findings: Overall, 32.1% of patients tested positive for opioid use. Post-UDT MOUD use was low (5.3% overall; 9.4% among those with positive opioid UDT). Multivariable logistic regression modeling showed that a positive opioid UDT was associated with more than twice the odds of post-UDT MOUD use (OR = 2.15; 95% CI = 2.10-2.20). However, among patients with post-UDT MOUD, positive opioid UDT was associated with lower odds of MOUD adherence (OR = 0.51; 95% CI = 0.49-0.54). Results were consistent for patients with diagnosed OUD.

Conclusions: Positive opioid UDT was associated with increased likelihood of post-UDT MOUD use but low MOUD treatment adherence. These findings highlight opportunities to strengthen sustained engagement with evidence-based treatment and underscore the need for care models that better support patients following opioid UDT, including timely MOUD use and adherence support.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Sociodemographic and intersecting sociodemographic subgroups in relation to US adult tobacco use trajectories over a 10-year period: Analysis of Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) data
item.description:
Introduction: Limited research has assessed tobacco use trajectories among subpopulations, particularly those representing intersecting minority identities, across adulthood. This study assessed tobacco use trajectories over 10 years among sociodemographic subgroups of US adults.

Methods: We analyzed 7 waves of data (2013-2022) from the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH). General growth mixture modeling assessed trajectories of any past-month use of cigarettes, e-cigarettes, cigars, hookah, and smokeless tobacco. Multivariable multinomial logistic regression assessed sociodemographics and sociodemographic interactions in relation to trajectory.

Results: Four trajectories were identified: "consistently low" (68.0% of participants) with low prevalence over time (0.7%-2.7 "consistently high" (21.6%) with 95-99% using at each wave; "medium increasing" (4.5%) which increased from 23% using at W1-60% at W7; and "steep decreasing" (5.9%) which decreased from 88% using at W1-6% at W7. Factors associated with being in the latter 3 trajectories vs. "consistently low" included being younger, male, sexual minority (SM), Black, and less educated. Factors associated with "steep decreasing" or "consistently high" vs. "medium increasing" included being older and White vs. Black; being male, non-Hispanic, and less educated was also associated with "consistently high". Factors associated with "consistently high" vs. "steep decreasing" included being older, non-Hispanic, and less educated. Significant interactions indicated certain intersecting identities (e.g., female and SM, SM and Black, Black/another race and Hispanic) more likely showed the latter 3 trajectories.

Conclusion: Tobacco prevention and intervention efforts must attend to sociodemographic profiles of adults at greatest risk for persistent or escalating tobacco use.

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: Decreasing response phase lights and siren use through modification of dispatch priority response for 9-1-1 responses to personal emergency response system activations: an interventional study
item.description:
Objectives: Emergency medical services (EMS) responses to personal emergency response systems (PERS) activations predominantly involve low-acuity patients. Recent evidence demonstrates that while most PERS calls are dispatched lights and siren (L&S), only 1% result in L&S transport. Reduction of L&S use through modified dispatch priority response for PERS calls has not been evaluated. Our objective was to evaluate the efficacy of modifying dispatch priority response mode for PERS calls to non-L&S response, the resulting reduction in response phase L&S use, and potential impact on time critical interventions.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational pre-post analysis comparing PERS responses in two 11-month periods before (January-November 2023) and after (January-November 2024) revising the dispatch priority response for PERS calls to non-L&S in December 2023. We evaluated response mode and transport mode. The primary outcome was total hours/month of response phase L&S use, with L&S duration computed as the interval between unit dispatched and arrival (patient contact) or call cancellation. Descriptive statistics were computed followed by interrupted time series analysis (ITSA) to assess the impact of the intervention on the primary outcome and maintenance of the effect across the post-intervention period (p for post-intervention linear trend).

Results: Analysis included 3,262 PERS calls (pre-intervention = 1,634; post-intervention = 1,628). L&S response occurred in 98% (n = 1,601) of pre-intervention calls and 12% (n = 192) of post-intervention calls (p < 0.001). The prevalence of L&S transport was similar in both periods (0.9% vs 0.9%, p = 0.99). The ITSA revealed an immediate 13.8-hour/month decrease in response phase L&S use (95% confidence interval: -16.2 to -11.3) that was sustained across the post-intervention period (p > 0.05). Total response phase L&S hours decreased 86%, from 172 hours in the pre-intervention period to 24 hours during the post-intervention period. Importantly, only four post-intervention calls (0.2%) involved a non-L&S response followed by L&S transport, with just one of these requiring advanced life support interventions.

Conclusions: Modifying dispatch priority response for PERS calls reduced L&S responses and yielded a marked decrease in hours of L&S use which was maintained overtime. As the industry advocates for safer, more judicious L&S use, additional low-acuity call types should be identified for similar dispatch priority response revision.

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: Prehospital Risk Stratification for Early Transfusion in Pediatric Trauma: A National Trauma Data Bank Analysis
item.description:
Objectives: Pediatric criteria remain limited for identifying injured children who may benefit from early blood transfusion for hemorrhagic shock. This study evaluated whether emergency medical services (EMS)-observable variables in a national trauma registry could identify children at risk for early hospital blood transfusion.

Methods: We conducted an observational retrospective cohort study using the National Trauma Data Bank (2017-2020). Among 391,126 records for patients aged 1-15 years, we included children transported by EMS directly from the scene to a participating trauma center after excluding burn injuries, interfacility transfers, and missing pre-identified EMS variables (systolic blood pressure, heart rate, or Glasgow Coma Scale [GCS]). The primary outcome was any blood product administered within 4 hours of emergency department arrival. Five prespecified EMS-observable predictors composed the model: age-adjusted hypotension, age-adjusted tachycardia, GCS ≤14, penetrating mechanism, and prehospital traumatic cardiac arrest. We fit a multivariable logistic regression and a classification and regression tree (CART) using an 80/20 stratified train-validation split. Missing data sensitivity analyses included multiple imputation and CART refitting in the broader eligible cohort.

Results: Among 79,764 children, 2,634 (3.3%) received early transfusion in the hospital. All five predictors were independently associated with early transfusion, led by GCS ≤14 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 8.38; 95% confidence interval [CI], 7.61-9.22), penetrating mechanism (aOR 5.87; 95% CI, 5.28-6.51), and age-adjusted hypotension (aOR 5.39; 95% CI, 4.74-6.13). In the validation cohort, CART analysis stratified patients into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk tiers comprising 77.0%, 19.7%, and 3.3% of patients, respectively. Early-transfusion rates were 1.2%, 6.1%, and 36.7% across these tiers. The high-risk tier accounted for 36.8% of all early transfusion events. Using the high-risk tier as a decision threshold, sensitivity was 36.8%, specificity 97.8%, positive predictive value 36.7%, and negative predictive value 97.8%.

Conclusions: Five EMS-observable features, including age-adjusted hypotension, age-adjusted tachycardia, GCS ≤14, penetrating mechanism, and prehospital traumatic cardiac arrest, identified a small subgroup of pediatric trauma patients with substantially elevated risk of early hospital transfusion. This parsimonious framework may inform prospective validation of prehospital transfusion criteria.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Homicide Mortality Among Female Adolescents and Women Aged 15 to 44 Years and US State Abortion Policies
item.description:
Importance: Homicide is a leading cause of death among female adolescents and women aged 15 to 44 years (hereinafter, women of reproductive age) in the US. Whether homicide trajectories differed across state abortion policy environments after the COVID-19 surge and the Dobbs v Jackson Women's Health Organization (hereinafter, Dobbs) decision is unclear.

Objectives: To characterize national homicide trends among women of reproductive age and assess whether post-2022 trajectories in homicide mortality among women of reproductive age diverged between states with and without sustained abortion bans.

Design, setting, and participants: This quasi-experimental study used national interrupted time series and comparative interrupted time series analyses of homicide mortality from January 1, 2016, through December 31, 2024, among women of reproductive age.

Exposure: The COVID-19 pandemic and sustained state abortion bans after Dobbs.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcome was monthly homicide deaths. The population-offset Poisson model estimated differential post-Dobbs changes in homicide rates. Absolute rate differences, excess deaths, and years of life lost were estimated from fitted and counterfactual Poisson models. States with sustained total or near-total abortion bans after Dobbs were compared with states without such bans; states with partial or legally fluid restrictions were excluded. A triple-difference analysis comparing those aged 15 to 29 years with those aged 45 to 59 years served as a negative-control analysis.

Results: The analysis included 19 118 homicide deaths among women of reproductive age. Nationally, homicide increased sharply during the COVID-19 surge and subsequently decreased, with no clear national level or slope change beginning in July 2022. In policy-stratified analyses, however, homicide trajectories diverged. After July 2022, the exposed states (those with total or near-total abortion bans) vs unexposed states homicide monthly rate ratio (RR) was 1.006 (95% CI, 1.000-1.011; P = .03). Across calendar years 2023 and 2024, the fitted homicide rate in exposed states was higher than the modeled counterfactual (2023: RR, 1.07; 95% bootstrap interval, 1.01-1.13; and 2024: RR, 1.15; 95% bootstrap interval, 1.03-1.29). This corresponded to an estimated 48 excess deaths (95% bootstrap interval, 11-81) in 2023 and 87 excess deaths (95% bootstrap interval, 20-149) in 2024. A triple-difference model indicated greater post-Dobbs divergence among those aged 15 to 29 years than those aged 45 to 59 years (monthly ratio of RRs, 1.017; 95% CI, 1.000-1.034; P = .046); placebo Dobbs dates yielded nonsignificant results.

Conclusions and relevance: In this study, national homicide mortality rates among women of reproductive age returned toward prepandemic levels after COVID-19, but post-2022 trajectories diverged across state abortion policy environments. The findings suggest that national improvements in homicide mortality rates among women of reproductive age may mask less-favorable homicide trends among women of reproductive age in states with sustained abortion bans.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Clinical Decision Support for Fall Prevention in Primary Care: The eSTEPS Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Falls are a leading cause of injury among older adults. Although exercise reduces fall risk, implementation in primary care remains limited.

Objective: To assess whether an electronic health record-integrated clinical decision support intervention, Electronic Strategies for Tailored Exercise to Prevent Falls (eSTEPS), reduces falls among older primary care patients at increased risk.

Design, setting, and participants: This matched-pair cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted from June 9, 2023, to May 8, 2025, with 12 to 23 months of follow-up at primary care practices within an integrated health system in the US. Adults aged 65 years or older with a positive 3-item fall-risk screen at a primary care visit were included.

Intervention: eSTEPS decision support embedded in the electronic health record with tailored exercise recommendations, optional physical therapy referral, and patient-facing materials (handouts, website, and app).

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the rate of patients with 1 or more falls identified using electronic health record-derived International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) diagnostic codes. Secondary outcomes were the rate of patients with 1 or more fall-related injuries identified by validated ICD-10 algorithms and mortality.

Results: Among 11 945 participants (mean [SD] age, 77.05 [7.43] years; 8044 females [67.3%]), of whom 5681 (47.6%) were in the intervention group and 6264 (52.4%) were in the control group, at 22 primary care practices, the rate of 1 or more ICD-10-coded falls (including falls with injuries) per 100 patient-years over the study period was 19.3 (95% CI, 18.6-20.1) in patients from intervention practices vs 21.2 (95% CI, 20.2-22.1) in patients from control practices (rate ratio [RR], 0.91 [95% CI, 0.88-0.95]; P < .001). The rate of ICD-10-coded fall-related injuries per 100 patient-years was 15.7 (95% CI, 15.0-16.5) from intervention practices vs 16.7 (95% CI, 16.1-17.4) from control practices over the study period (RR for fall injuries per 100 patient-years, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.90-0.97]; P = .001). No differences were observed in mortality. For intervention patients, eSTEPS exercise prescriptions were issued for 1255 patients (22.1%). Overall, 215 clinicians (77.9%) in intervention practices used the clinical decision support to deliver the exercise program at least once over the study period.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cluster randomized clinical trial of an electronic health record-integrated decision support, falls and fall-related injuries were modestly reduced in older adults in primary care. These results suggest support for scalable, workflow-integrated fall prevention.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04993781.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Substance Misuse Prevalence and Risk Factors in Adolescents and Young Adults With Depression
item.description:
Importance: The prevalence of youths with mental health conditions has increased in recent years. Youths with mental health conditions are at risk of substance misuse via coping and self-regulation pathways; there is therefore a need to identify and address barriers to integrated mental health and substance use treatment in these youths.

Objective: To examine the prevalence of and motivations for prescription psychotherapeutic drug misuse among youths with and without depression.

Design, setting, and participants: A cross-sectional analysis of the 2023 and 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH) using a nationally representative survey of noninstitutionalized individuals aged 12 years and older related to drugs of misuse and mental health disorders. Data on adolescents and young adults were analyzed from January to March 2026.

Exposure: Past-year major depressive episode (MDE).

Main outcomes and measure: The primary outcome was past-year prescription psychotherapeutic drug misuse and use disorder, and the secondary outcome was motivations for misuse. Survey-weighted prevalence estimates with 95% CIs were calculated and group differences were assessed using χ2 tests. To assess the association between drug misuse and depression, logistic regression models were used.

Results: The 2023 and 2024 NSDUH included 22 906 adolescents (aged 12-17 years) and 27 723 young adults (aged 18-25 years), among whom 24 831 (49.1%) were males, 13 256 (26.2%) were Hispanic, 6923 (13.7%) were non-Hispanic Black, 23 114 (45.6%) were non-Hispanic White, and 7336 (14.5%) were non-Hispanic-all other races. A past-year MDE was reported by 16.3% (95% CI, 15.6%-17.0%) of respondents, corresponding to an estimated 9.8 million individuals nationally. Among youths with a past-year MDE, 6.6% (95% CI, 5.8%-7.5%) reported misuse of psychotherapeutic drugs while 6.0% (95% CI, 5.2%-6.9%) reported use disorder. Youths with a past-year MDE had significantly higher odds of reporting prescription drug misuse (odds ratio [OR], 2.09; 95% CI, 1.75-2.50) and prescription drug use disorder (OR, 4.02; 95% CI, 3.37-4.80) compared with those without a past-year MDE. Compared with youths without a past-year MDE, youths with a past-year MDE were more likely to report misusing opioid analgesics (10.2% [95% CI, 6.4%-15.9%] vs 3.7% [95% CI, 2.2%-6.3%]; P = .01) and tranquilizers (29.8% [95% CI, 21.1%-40.3%] vs 13.2% [95% CI, 5.8%-19.9%]; P = .003) to help with feelings and emotions.

Conclusions and relevance: This cross-sectional analysis of the 2023 and 2024 NSDUH found that youths with depression were more likely than their peers without depression both to report prescription drug misuse and to meet criteria for prescription drug use disorder. For certain medications, this misuse was more often motivated by a desire to address feelings and emotions. These findings underscore the need to identify and address barriers to integrated mental health and substance use treatment for at-risk youths before patterns of self-medication progress to enduring substance use disorders.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Preterm Risk Factors, Epigenetic Age, and Neurodevelopmental Outcomes
item.description:
Importance: Studies examining biological factors associated with neurodevelopment in the preterm population are limited. It was previously demonstrated that epigenetic age acceleration was associated with better neurodevelopmental outcomes among children born preterm. It is unclear whether this association is modified by clinical and environmental preterm risk factors.

Objective: To examine whether the association between epigenetic aging and neurodevelopmental outcomes is modified by preterm brain injury and socioeconomic status.

Design, setting, and participants: This was a prospective cohort study of children born at 24 to 32 weeks' gestation, recruited from 2 neonatal intensive care units from 2015 to 2019 and followed up to January 2026. The cohort was well characterized with clinical data, brain magnetic resonance imaging, and neurodevelopmental assessments (Bayley-III cognitive and motor domains) at 3 years. Participants with buccal epithelial cell DNA collected at 3 years were included.

Exposure: Epigenetic age (in weeks) at 3 years was determined using the pediatric buccal epigenetic clock and corrected for chronological age to give epigenetic age difference.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary analyses used linear regression to examine the association between epigenetic age difference, preterm risk factors (any brain injury, severe brain injury, maternal educational level), and cognitive and motor outcomes at 3 years. Secondary analyses examined whether brain injury and maternal education level modified the associations between epigenetic age difference and cognitive and motor outcomes at 3 years.

Results: A total of 102 study participants (median gestational age, 27.0 weeks [IQR, 25.6-28.9 weeks]; 54 female [53%]) were included. Higher maternal educational level (β = 11.65; 95% CI, 3.55-19.76; P = .005) and epigenetic age acceleration (β = 0.07; 95% CI, 0.01-0.14; P = .04) were associated with higher cognitive scores. Epigenetic age acceleration was also associated with higher motor scores (β = 0.16; 95% CI, 0.06-0.27; P = .003), while extreme prematurity (β = -5.66; 95% CI, -10.85 to -0.46; P = .03) and severe brain injury (β = -10.99; 95% CI, -21.32 to -0.66; P = .04) were associated with lower motor scores. Severe brain injury modified the association between epigenetic aging and motor outcomes (β = 0.41; 95% CI, 0.08-0.74; P = .02), and children with epigenetic age acceleration in the presence of severe brain injury had higher motor scores.

Conclusions and relevance: In this prospective preterm cohort study, epigenetic aging, severe brain injury, and socioeconomic status were associated with neurodevelopmental outcomes. Children with severe brain injury along with epigenetic age acceleration had higher motor scores. These findings suggest the association between epigenetic aging and neurodevelopment is context dependent and can vary based on the presence of preterm risk factors.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Cervical Cancer Screening Rates by Race and Ethnicity, Age, Language, and Census Region
item.description:
Importance: Longitudinal evidence of cervical cancer screening (CCS) trends before and after COVID-19 across demographic cohorts remains limited.

Objective: To examine CCS rates by race and ethnicity, age, language, and census region among patients with at least 1 health care encounter in an electronic medical record (EMR) system from 2019 through 2024, and to evaluate longitudinal trends across these groups.

Design, setting, and participants: Using an EMR database, this cross-sectional study evaluated CCS rates among female patients aged 21 to 64 years between 2019 and 2024, stratified by race and ethnicity, age, language, and census region.

Exposures: Race and ethnicity, age, language, and census region.

Main outcomes and measures: Descriptive statistics were used to summarize annual CCS rates across demographic groups. The Cochran-Armitage test assessed linear trends over time.

Results: Annual sample sizes ranged from approximately 9 to 16 million patients and increased steadily over time; analytic population sizes varied across subgroups. Most patients were non-Hispanic White, aged 30 to 49 years, English-speaking, and resided in either the South or Northeast. Non-Hispanic White patients had the highest annual CCS rates from 2019 to 2021 but experienced the smallest percentage increase, from 10.98% (95% CI, 10.96%-11.01%) to 13.85% (95% CI, 13.82%-13.87%), over the study period. Hispanic patients experienced the largest percentage increase in CCS rates, from 9.85% (95% CI, 9.80%-9.90%) to 15.51% (95% CI, 15.47%-15.55%). American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander patients had the lowest screening rates throughout the study period. Patients aged 30 to 49 years and non-English-speaking patients consistently had the highest CCS rates across all years. Patients in the Western and Southern census regions had lower CCS rates than those in other regions.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of patients with at least 1 health care encounter in an EMR system, all CCS rates increased across all racial and ethnic groups from 2019 to 2024, with the greatest gains observed among Hispanic patients. However, persistent disparities remained, particularly among American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander patients and those in the Western and Southern regions. These findings suggest that although screening uptake has improved over time, substantial geographic and racial and ethnic disparities in CCS persist, highlighting important areas for future research and intervention efforts.

item.title: Crit Care Med: A Quality Improvement Initiative to Achieve Provincial Implementation of a Web-Based Family Satisfaction in ICU (FS-ICU) Survey to Inform Patient-Centered Care
item.description:
Objectives: To review the web-based Family Satisfaction in ICU (FS-ICU) survey across all adult level 3 Ontario ICUs to capture patient and family experiences with critical care, and to evaluate feasibility, participation, and satisfaction scores.

Design: A province-wide, multisite quality improvement study using an electronic, key-based FS-ICU survey with prospectively collected anonymous data linked to encounters through a centralized database.

Setting: All 83 adult level 3 ICUs (52 community, 31 academic) in ON, Canada, from July 1, 2019, to May 31, 2024.

Patients: The population comprised adult ICU patients, family members, or substitute decision-makers, with one survey per ICU encounter regardless of length of stay or number of family members.

Interventions: ICUs implemented a web-based FS-ICU using a unique seven-digit key in three formats (Staff-Provided, Quick Response-Driven, Website-Code), supported by training, resources, and tablets, with no clinical care interventions beyond routine practice.

Measurements and main results: Feasibility metrics included onboarding (keys generated per ICU admission), opening, participation, and completion rates, calculated for different centers using provincial data. Over the study period, 24,679 unique keys were generated for 353,400 ICU admissions (onboarding rate, 7.0%), 13,596 keys were opened (opening rate, 55.1%), and 7,542 surveys met the greater than or equal to 70% completion threshold (completion rate, 57.6% among opened surveys; reflection rate, 2.1% of ICU encounters). Survey initiation was highest with the Staff-Provided format (88.4% of keys initiated), and overall satisfaction was high, with mean FS with Care, 87.8; FS with Decision-Making, 84.4; and FS-TOTAL 86.5 on a 0-100 scale, with nursing care rated highest and adequacy of time for questions rated lowest.

Conclusions: A provincial, web-based FS-ICU was implemented across all adult level 3 Ontario ICUs, producing a large dataset with high satisfaction scores. A small proportion completed the survey, highlighting feasibility and workflow barriers. Future efforts should improve activation and completion rates and integrate FS-ICU data into routine quality improvement to enhance patient- and family-centered care.

item.title: Crit Care Med: ICU Physical Environments Used for Family Conferences: A Multimodal Qualitative Evaluation with ICU Team Members
item.description:
Objectives: Family-clinician communication is central to high-quality care for critically ill patients. Although previous work has focused on improving how and what is communicated, little is known about where this high-stakes communication takes place and how it is shaped by the physical environment. Our objectives were to characterize ICU spaces typically used for family conferences and identify modifiable environmental features that influence communication.

Design: We conducted a multimodal qualitative study of 17 spaces typically used for family conferences across four adult ICUs in a U.S. academic medical center. Healthcare design and architecture experts independently assessed architectural plans and photographs to characterize spatial features. Then, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 23 ICU team members (nurses, social workers, case managers) to elicit perspectives on and experiences within these spaces. We conducted qualitative content analysis using a combined inductive and deductive approach.

Setting: A total of 17 family conference spaces across four adult ICUs in a U.S. academic medical center.

Participants: A total of 23 ICU team members.

Interventions: None.

Results: The 17 analyzed spaces included designated family-communication rooms (n = 2), multipurpose rooms (n = 6), visitor lounges (n = 4), and public areas (n = 5; lobbies/hallways). Study participants preferred designated spaces, as they provide privacy, prevent interruption, and facilitate emotional support. Conversely, multipurpose and public areas are prone to distractions and interruptions from conflicting uses. We identified key environmental features that support communication: proximity to patients, flexible furniture layout, and nonclinical ambiance.

Conclusions: Family conferences occur in a variety of physical environments in and around adult ICUs, ranging from intentionally designed rooms to elevator lobbies. ICU team members perceive that physical environments have an important influence on communication quality, and we identified pragmatic opportunities to improve existing spaces.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Emergency medicine updates: Contrast media hypersensitivity
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Contrast media hypersensitivity reaction is a rare but clinically significant condition that can meaningfully affect emergency department (ED) patient care. Therefore, it is important for emergency medicine clinicians to be aware of the current evidence regarding the diagnosis, prevention, and management of this condition.

Objective: This paper evaluates key evidence-based updates concerning contrast media hypersensitivity reactions for the emergency clinician.

Discussion: Adverse reactions to contrast media are divided into common physiologic reactions and less common hypersensitivity reactions. Hypersensitivity reactions can be immediate or delayed, ranging from mild urticaria to anaphylaxis. The greatest risk factor for hypersensitivity reaction to contrast media is a prior hypersensitivity reaction to contrast media. It is crucial to discern and document the specific culprit agent, severity, type, and timing of previous and current reactions. Physiologic reactions can be treated with supportive care and usually self-resolve. Acute evaluation and treatment of moderate-to-severe hypersensitivity reactions mirrors standard anaphylaxis care, with intramuscular epinephrine as the first-line drug for severe reactions, and allergist referral should be considered. Patients with a prior physiologic reaction do not require premedication or contrast switching. For prevention of breakthrough hypersensitivity reactions, switching to a chemically different contrast agent is more effective than corticosteroid premedication. Routine corticosteroid premedication is no longer recommended, as literature has not demonstrated corticosteroid pretreatment reduces hypersensitivity reactions. Second-generation antihistamines may be of benefit for patients with a history of mild-moderate reactions. Severe or anaphylactic reactions warrant strong consideration of alternative imaging. Collaboration with key stakeholders, including radiology and pharmacy, is important to improve workflows, protocols, and patient care.

Conclusions: An understanding of literature updates can improve the ED care of patients with contrast media hypersensitivity reactions.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Peripheral perfusion index for differentiating cardiac and pulmonary dyspnea in the emergency department: A prospective observational study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Dyspnea is a common reason for emergency department (ED) visits, often caused by cardiac or pulmonary conditions with overlapping clinical presentations. Rapid differentiation between these etiologies is crucial for timely management and prognosis. The peripheral perfusion index (PPI), derived from pulse oximetry, has emerged as a non-invasive biomarker of tissue perfusion. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of PPI in distinguishing cardiac from pulmonary causes of dyspnea and to assess its prognostic value for clinical outcomes.

Methods: We conducted a prospective observational study in the adult ED of Ankara Etlik City Hospital between March 1 and March 31, 2025. Adult patients presenting with dyspnea were consecutively enrolled, with predefined exclusion criteria applied. Demographic data, vital signs, laboratory parameters, and PPI values were collected within 30 min of presentation. Final diagnoses were established using clinical, laboratory, imaging findings, and specialist consultation. The primary outcome was the diagnostic accuracy of PPI in differentiating cardiac and pulmonary dyspnea. Secondary outcomes included ED disposition and 30-day mortality.

Results: A total of 320 patients were included (median age: 73 years; 56.9% female). Pulmonary diseases accounted for 55.9% (n = 179), and cardiac diseases for 44.1% (n = 141). Median PPI was significantly lower in the cardiac group compared with the pulmonary group (1.8 [IQR 1.2-2.2] vs. 2.8 [IQR 2.0-4.3]; p < 0.001). PPI values were also lower in patients admitted to the ICU (1.5) and in 30-day non-survivors (1.5) compared with discharged patients (4.1; p < 0.001). Receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated good diagnostic performance for pulmonary disease prediction (AUC: 0.801; 95% CI: 0.749-0.844), with an optimal cutoff of >2.2 (sensitivity 71%, specificity 74%).

Conclusion: PPI is a simple, non-invasive, and rapidly obtainable parameter that may aid in differentiating cardiac from pulmonary causes of dyspnea in the ED. Lower PPI values were observed in patients with cardiac-origin dyspnea and were associated with ICU admission and 30-day mortality; however, the prognostic findings should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for residual confounding.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Nationwide trends of six medications for alcohol use disorder prescriptions post-discharge in patients hospitalized with alcohol-associated liver disease between 2015 and 2024
item.description:
Introduction: Alcohol associated liver disease (ALD) carries a high risk of hospitalization and recidivism, yet post-discharge medications for alcohol use disorder (MAUD) are not universally prescribed. MAUD prescriptions have been associated with reduced recidivism and hepatic decompensation. However, national data on prescribing patterns is limited. We examined ten-year trends in six MAUD prescriptions after hospitalization for ALD.

Methods: We identified 150,241 US adults hospitalized with ALD between 2015 and 2024 using electronic health records from TriNetX. Outcomes included annual prevalence, incidence rate, and incidence proportion of post-discharge MAUD prescriptions. FDA-approved agents included disulfiram, acamprosate, and naltrexone; off-label agents included topiramate, baclofen, and gabapentin. Trends were assessed using Joinpoint regression with annual percentage change (APC) and average annual percentage change (AAPC). Subgroup analyses were stratified by cirrhosis status and sex.

Results: FDA-approved MAUD had consistently lower prescription rates than off-label agents over the past decade. From 2015-2024, disulfiram was the only FDA-approved agent with a declining trend, while acamprosate (AAPC 20.35%) and naltrexone (AAPC 17.83%) demonstrated significant increases for new prescriptions. By 2024, the prevalence of FDA-approved and off-label MAUD prescriptions were 17.98% and 41.96%, respectively. Patients with cirrhosis had lower prescribing rates but exhibited greater relative increases in FDA-approved MAUD prescriptions. Women were more likely to receive off-label prescriptions, though both sexes showed similar upward trends.

Conclusion: Post-discharge MAUD prescribing for ALD has risen significantly, but less than 20% of patients receive FDA-approved MAUD. Expanding access to evidence-based medications is critical to improve outcomes in this high-risk population.

Background: There are no estimates of incident opioid use disorder (OUD), using current diagnostic criteria, among patients prescribed long-term opioid therapy (LtOT). Purpose: To estimate changes in buprenorphine use among Kentucky Medicaid enrollees with opioid use disorder (OUD) after policy changes and pandemic disruptions, and whether impacts differed by county-level context, primarily rurality and, secondarily, opioid treatment program (OTP) availability.

Methods: We analyzed Kentucky Medicaid claims from January 2018 through June 2025, identifying enrollees with diagnosed OUD to construct 10,800 county-month observations. Logistic regression fitted with weighted generalized estimating equations was used for statistical modeling of an interrupted time series (ITS) design to assess changes in the monthly proportion of enrollees with OUD receiving buprenorphine. Interruptions included removal of prior authorization (PA) requirements for transmucosal buprenorphine, methadone coverage initiation, COVID-19-related policy changes, and federal X-waiver elimination. Rurality and OTP availability were evaluated as effect modifiers.

Results: The proportion of enrollees with OUD receiving buprenorphine increased from 0.29 to 0.45 across the study period. PA removal was associated with an immediate increase in the odds of buprenorphine use (odds ratio [OR]=1.043; 95% confidence interval [CI]=1.025, 1.061), corresponding to a 1.4-percentage-point increase. X-waiver elimination was associated with a sustained increase in trend (OR 1.007; 95% CI 1.004-1.010). Differential effects by rurality were limited to the COVID-19 period. Counties without an OTP responded more strongly to PA removal than counties with an OTP (P = 0.037).

Conclusions: Removal of administrative and regulatory barriers was associated with increased buprenorphine use among Kentucky Medicaid enrollees with OUD, with effects varying by county-level context, particularly OTP availability.

item.title: JAMA: Clinician Use of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Clinical Information Platform
item.description:
Importance: Despite growing interest in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine, empirical evidence on how clinicians use these tools is limited.

Objective: To characterize clinician use of an AI-enabled clinical information platform, the distribution of use across the clinical workforce, and the purpose of submitted queries.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study analyzed clinicians with National Provider Identifier-verified accounts of a commonly used AI-enabled clinical information platform, OpenEvidence, from January 1, 2024, through June 30, 2026. A large language model was used to classify the clinical purpose and topic areas of a stratified random sample of 38.8 million queries.

Main outcomes and measures: The number of active users and clinical queries, the share of queries relative to representation in the national workforce, and the clinical purpose and topic of queries were examined.

Results: Overall, 952 008 clinicians (58.5% female), including 556 200 physicians, submitted 271 million queries during the 2.5-year study period. Monthly active users increased from 355 in January 2024 to 703 265 in June 2026, and average monthly queries per active user rose from 18.0 to 39.5. Nurse practitioners (44.5) and physician assistants (44.5) submitted more queries per active user-month than physicians (37.1). A higher share of queries relative to the national workforce was submitted by physicians within a decade of graduation (use ratio, 2.54) and residents and fellows (1.84). Use was also higher than average among physicians specializing in oncology and hematology (use ratio, 2.00), internal medicine (1.88), and family medicine (1.80), but lower in procedural and diagnostic specialties (ophthalmology, 0.23; radiology, 0.24; orthopedics, 0.24). Most queries addressed clinical decision-making (51.9%), particularly treatment and management (33.1%), whereas diagnosis accounted for 13.9% of queries. Queries addressing topics outside physicians' own specialties ranged from 35% among oncologists and hematologists to 88% among emergency department physicians.

Conclusions and relevance: Over 2.5 years, more than 950 000 US clinicians submitted greater than 270 million queries to an AI-enabled clinical information platform. Use varied across clinician types, specialties, and career stages and was frequently for treatment decisions rather than diagnostic tasks.

item.description:
Importance: Laser therapy is increasingly used to treat genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) in breast cancer survivors, but sham-controlled evidence of benefit remains limited.

Objective: To evaluate 12-month efficacy and safety of fractional carbon dioxide (CO2) laser therapy (CLT) vs sham laser therapy (SLT) for GSM in breast cancer survivors receiving aromatase inhibitors.

Design, setting, and participants: This is a secondary analysis of a single-center, double-blind, sham-controlled randomized clinical trial conducted at a tertiary academic hospital in Spain. Participants included breast cancer survivors with GSM and dyspareunia receiving aromatase inhibitors, recruited from October 30, 2020, to September 1, 2021. Participants were followed up for 12 months. Data were analyzed from December 1, 2024, to June 30, 2025.

Intervention: Five monthly sessions of CLT or SLT plus first-line nonhormonal therapy (FLT), including vaginal moisturizers and vibrators.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the between-group difference in change in Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) score. Secondary outcomes included rate of sexual activity, dyspareunia, Spanish Body Image Scale, quality of life (12-Item Short Form Health Survey), Vaginal Health Index, objective parameters (pH, vaginal maturation index, epithelial measures), serum estradiol level, FLT adherence, and adverse events.

Results: Of the 84 randomized participants (mean [SD] age, 53.8 [8.8] years), 67 completed the 12-month follow-up (CLT, 32; SLT, 35). The CLT group did not differ from the SLT group in FSFI score change from baseline to 12 months (difference, CLT vs SLT, -0.69 [95% CI, -3.58 to 2.20]; P = .64), nor in any secondary outcome. Across the full sample, significant improvements from baseline to 12 months were observed in FSFI score (18.9 to 23.0; mean difference, 4.5 [95% CI, 3.1-5.9]; P < .001), dyspareunia (mean difference, -3.7 [95% CI, -4.4 to -3.0]; P < .001), Spanish Body Image Scale (mean difference, -3.9 [95% CI, -5.1 to -2.8]; P < .001), and Vaginal Health Index (mean difference, 4.2 [95% CI, 3.1-5.2]; P < .001). Sexual activity increased among 57 of 67 participants (85.1%; odds ratio, 2.35 [95% CI, 1.23-4.50]; P = .009). Improvements were found in pH (mean difference, -0.5 [95% CI, -0.8 to -0.2]; P < .001) and vaginal maturation index (mean difference, 19.0% [95% CI, 13.4%-24.5%]; P < .001). FLT adherence was similar between groups. No severe adverse effects occurred.

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial of breast cancer survivors receiving aromatase inhibitors, vulvovaginal CLT provided no additional benefit for sexual or vaginal health at 12 months. Improvements in both groups likely reflected FLT adherence, trial participation, or contextual factors rather than laser efficacy. High-quality sham-controlled trials remain essential before routine implementation.

item.description:
Importance: Data on quality of life (QOL) after total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) are important for counseling patients on the benefits of watch-and-wait (WW) vs total mesorectal excision (TME) for rectal cancer. A thorough understanding of both options and their long-term impact on bowel, urinary, sexual function, and other QOL domains remains limited.

Objective: To examine the association of organ preservation with QOL and functional outcomes among patients with rectal cancer treated in 2 phase 2 clinical trials.

Design, setting, and participants: This unplanned, post hoc, cohort study used data from the CAO/ARO/AIO-12 and CAO/ARO/AIO-16 trials, recruiting participants from June 15, 2015, through October 7, 2020, from 19 centers in Germany. Included patients had cT3 to cT4 or node-positive rectal adenocarcinoma. Total neoadjuvant treatment included chemoradiation therapy combined with induction or consolidation chemotherapy. The statistical analysis was performed from March 6 to December 23, 2025.

Main outcomes and measures: The association of WW with functional outcomes and QOL was assessed using prospectively recorded EORTC QLQ-C30, EORTC QLQ-CR29, and Wexner score questionnaires. Differences in QOL scores were estimated using adjusted longitudinal and cross-sectional analyses with a predefined clinically meaningful difference of at least 5 points.

Results: Baseline questionnaires were available from 346 of 385 eligible patients (89.9%; median [range] age, 60 [19-80] years; 257 male [67%]), while available QOL questionnaires decreased over time to 185 (48.1%) at 5 years. Using the longitudinal analytic approach, statistically significant and clinically meaningful differences in favor of WW were noted for fecal incontinence (-21.2 [95% CI, -30.0 to -12.3]; P < .001); stool frequency (-19.8 [95% CI, -27.6 to -11.9]; P < .001); embarrassment (-17.0 [95% CI, -27.4 to -6.6]; P = .002); flatulence (-15.2 [95% CI, -24.4 to -6.0]; P < .001), buttock pain (-11.9 [95% CI, -20.8 to -3.0]; P = .01); social (9.7 [95% CI, 1.1-18.3]; P = .03), physical (10.2 [95% CI, 4.1-16.3]; P = .002), and role (13.9 [95% CI, 4.9-22.9]; P = .003) functioning; and global health status (9.2 [95% CI, 3.2-15.2]; P = .004). These clinically meaningful differences were detectable in both the intended organ preservation and disease-free groups. Patients with sustained clinical complete response at 3 years (n = 29) vs those with pathologic complete response or matched baseline characteristics favored WW for fecal incontinence (-24.0 and -11.6, respectively), stool frequency (-34.6 and -19.1), sore skin (-18.0 and -18.1), buttock pain (-14.7 and -17.6), embarrassment (-41.1 and -20.5), role functioning (19.1 and 10.9), and social functioning (20.0 and 8.4).

Conclusions and relevance: In the absence of prospective randomized trials, this study provides evidence suggesting long-term clinically meaningful benefits for organ preservation regarding QOL, especially for most gastrointestinal subscales, social functioning, and global health status, over a 5-year period among patients with rectal cancer. item.description:
Importance: Low socioeconomic status is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease, yet it remains unclear whether this association has changed over time. Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) are key contributors to cardiovascular morbidity, mortality, and health care costs and, thus, are indicators of the overall cardiovascular burden.

Objective: To describe temporal trends in incident MACE by equivalized income groups in the Danish population from 1988 to 2023.

Design, setting, and participants: This nationwide, population-based open cohort study using data from Danish national registries included all residents of Denmark aged 30 years or older who were alive in each year between January 1, 1988, and January 1, 2023, and had available income observations in the current or preceding 5 years. Individuals were followed up to December 31 of each year, to death, or to emigration. Data were analyzed from August 2025 to July 2026.

Exposure: Equivalized disposable household income.

Main outcome and measures: Incident MACE, defined as the first hospital admission for acute myocardial infarction, unstable angina, stroke, or heart failure. Age-standardized incidence rates were calculated annually, stratified by income quartile and sex.

Results: A total of 5 932 672 individuals aged 30 years or older were registered in the Danish Civil Registration System from 1988 to 2023. item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Ultraprocessed Food Intake and Adiposity, Vascular Brain Injury, and Cognition in Middle-Aged Adults
item.description:
Importance: Ultraprocessed foods (UPFs) account for a substantial and increasing proportion of dietary intake in Canada. Although UPFs are consistently associated with adiposity and cardiometabolic disease, their associations with subclinical vascular brain injury (VBI) and cognitive performance in midlife are unclear.

Objective: To evaluate associations of UPF consumption with adiposity, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-defined VBI, and cognitive performance in middle-aged adults in Canada.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study included 8783 adults aged 35 to 69 years without cardiovascular disease who were enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Healthy Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) studies. Participants from CAHHM were recruited from January 1, 2014, to December 31, 2018, and participants from PURE-MIND were recruited from January 1, 2010, to December 31, 2018. Data analyses were conducted between July 16, 2024, and August 16, 2026.

Exposures: UPF consumption assessed using previously validated semiquantitative food frequency questionnaires and expressed as servings per 2000 kcal/d.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcomes were body fat (BF) percentage (bioelectrical impedance), visceral adipose tissue (VAT) volume, hepatic fat fraction (HFF), VBI defined as covert brain infarcts or high white matter hyperintensities (HWMHs) (measured by MRI), and cognitive performance measured by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) and the Digital Symbol Substitution Test (DSST).

Results: In this cross-sectional study of 8783 participants (mean [SD] age, 57.7 [8.7] years; 4917 females [56.6%]), those in the highest quartile of UPF intake had a BF percentage that was 1.7 (95% CI, 1.2-2.2) percentage points higher and a 5.7 (95% CI, 3.2-8.3) mL greater VAT volume compared with those in the lowest quartile, but no significant difference in HFF. Compared with the lowest quartile, the highest UPF quartile had higher odds of VBI (adjusted OR, 1.40; 95% CI, 1.10-1.77; P for trend = .009). No significant associations were observed between UPF intake and MOCA or DSST performance.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of middle-aged adults in Canada, higher UPF intake was associated with greater adiposity and higher odds of MRI-defined VBI but not cognitive performance. Associations with VBI were sensitive to UPF exposure definition. Longitudinal studies are needed to establish temporality.

Both outcomes were censored at last follow-up and estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method with 95% CIs.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Disparities in α1-Antitrypsin Deficiency Testing and Treatment in US Adults
item.description:
Importance: α1-Antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) is underdiagnosed despite guidelines for broad testing, and the factors associated with low testing and treatment are not well known.

Objective: To identify factors associated with low AATD testing and augmentation therapy in individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma.

Design, setting, and participants: This is a retrospective, multicenter cohort study using national electronic health record data from the Veterans Health Administration from January 1, 2020, to December 31, 2024. Data analysis was conducted from July to October 2025. Participants were individuals with a diagnosis of COPD and/or asthma (≥2 International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, or International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision codes).

Exposure: Individual demographics, comorbidities, tobacco use, rural-urban residence, Social Vulnerability Index (SVI), and drive time to the specialty care facility.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcomes were prevalence of and factors associated with AATD testing and augmentation therapy prescription. Multivariable regression models were used, adjusting sequentially for demographics, comorbidities, tobacco use, rural-urban residence, SVI, and drive time to the specialty care facility.

Results: Among 2 384 913 individuals with COPD and/or asthma (mean [SD] age, 64.2 [14.3] years; 178 898 female [7.5%]; 16 778 [0.7%] American Indian or Alaska Native; 14 996 [0.7%] Asian; 331 202 Black or African American [15.3%]; 19 029 [0.9%] Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander; 1 787 951 White [82.4%]), 138 278 (5.8%) underwent testing. In fully adjusted models, cirrhosis (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 6.40; 95% CI, 6.29-6.51) and bronchiectasis (aOR, 3.73; 95% CI, 3.59-3.87) were associated with higher odds of testing. Older ages and active tobacco use were associated with lower odds of testing. Rural-urban residence and SVI had similar odds across categories. Longer drive times were associated with progressively lower odds of testing (>90 vs ≤30 minutes; aOR, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.62-0.65). Of 8564 with AATD diagnosis, 320 (3.7%) were prescribed augmentation therapy and showed a similar pattern as testing, occurring less often among patients from minoritized racial and ethnic groups, those actively using tobacco, and those with longer drive times to specialty care, and more often among those with cirrhosis and bronchiectasis.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of individuals with COPD and/or asthma, AATD testing and augmentation therapy were profoundly low. System-level reform is needed to bridge gaps across age, comorbidities, tobacco use, and health care access.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Prehospital Point-of-Care GFAP for Detection of Intracranial Hemorrhage in Acute Nontraumatic Coma
item.description:
Importance: Rapid identification of intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) in patients with acute nontraumatic coma is critical to guiding triage and early management; however, prehospital diagnostic tools remain limited.

Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of prehospital whole-blood point-of-care measurement of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and ubiquitin carboxy-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) for detecting ICH.

Design, setting, and participants: This diagnostic study used data collected by a UK physician-paramedic helicopter emergency medical service between January 1, 2025, and April 30, 2026. A consecutive sample of adult patients (aged ≥16 years) presenting with acute nontraumatic coma, defined as Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 12 or less, who underwent prehospital rapid sequence induction (RSI) of anesthesia with clinical suspicion of ICH were eligible for inclusion. Patients with traumatic pathology and those without follow-up data were excluded. Patients were observed for up for 30 days from hospital admission. Data analysis was performed in June 2026.

Exposure: Prehospital whole-blood point-of-care brain biomarker (GFAP and UCH-L1) testing using the i-STAT Alinity Point-of-Care Blood Analyzer (Abbott Laboratories).

Main outcome and measures: Diagnostic accuracy of GFAP and UCH-L1 for detecting ICH, using computed tomography as the reference standard. Sensitivity, specificity, predictive value, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) were calculated.

Results: The primary study cohort comprised 65 patients who underwent prehospital brain biomarker testing (median age, 63 [IQR, 47-69] years; 55.4% male). The median (IQR) GCS score was 4 (3-6). ICH was present in 50.8% (n = 33). Thirteen (20.0%) patients underwent neurosurgery, and the 30-day survival rate was 46.2% (n = 30). GFAP demonstrated high sensitivity (97.0%; 95% CI, 84.2%-99.9%) and discriminatory ability (AUC, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.87-0.99). UCH-L1 showed lower sensitivity (78.8%; 95% CI, 61.1%-91.0%) and specificity (18.8%; 95% CI, 7.2%-36.4%), with limited discriminatory performance. A combined biomarker approach achieved 100.0% sensitivity (95% CI, 89.4%-100.0%) and a negative predictive value of 100.0% (95% CI, 47.8%-100.0%).

Conclusions and relevance: In this diagnostic study of adults with acute nontraumatic coma undergoing prehospital RSI, point-of-care prehospital GFAP testing was feasible and demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy in detecting intracranial hemorrhage. Further prospective external validation is required to determine its association with triage, treatment decisions, and patient outcomes.

item.title: Ann Emerg Med: Adoption of Outpatient Management of Acute Low-Risk Pulmonary Embolism
item.description:
Study objective: To assess longitudinal outcomes of a multicomponent intervention designed to address key barriers to the outpatient management of low-risk pulmonary embolism (PE), and to define the most appropriate target population and metric for evaluating adoption.

Methods: We implemented a multicomponent intervention in the emergency department (ED) of a quaternary academic medical center. Outcomes were evaluated using the RE-AIM framework, comparing a 3-year preimplementation period (2016-2019) with active implementation (year I), postimplementation (year II), and maintenance (year III) periods. The primary outcome (adoption) was the proportion of low-PESI (≤85) patients discharged from the ED. Following implementation, the charts of all hospitalized low-PESI patients were reviewed to determine reasons for admission.

Results: Among 1,810 patients with acute PE, 705 (39.0%) had low-PESI scores. Adoption rose from 5.1% preimplementation to 16.1% (odds ratio [OR] 3.43, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.77 to 6.63), 24.0% (OR 5.98, 95% CI 3.04 to 11.78), and 33.3% (OR 9.24, 95% CI 5.04 to 16.92) in years I to III. There were no recurrent venous thromboembolism or deaths within 30 days of any ED discharge. Bleeding complications were rare (0%-4.3%) and none required hospitalization. Hospitalization decreased primarily among low-PESI patients without Hestia criteria, whereas admission of low-PESI Hestia-positive patients remained relatively constant. Excluding Hestia-positive cases, adoption increased from 9.0% preimplementation to 75% in the maintenance phase.

Conclusion: In this single-center implementation study, a multicomponent intervention guided by RE-AIM resulted in a sustained increase in outpatient management of low-risk PE. Both the PESI score and Hestia criteria could be incorporated into the definition of the target population and future quality metrics.

Objectives: This study evaluated the efficacy of different high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) weaning protocols in critically ill adults.

Design: This multicenter, randomized controlled trial was conducted from December 1, 2022, to August 31, 2024, based on the suggested protocol (SLOWH trial). Experts reviewed the trial between October 2, 2024, and April 15, 2025.

Setting: Randomization was performed by a research coordinator using a sequence of random numbers generated by an independent statistician blinded to both researchers and participants.

Background: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has been shown to be beneficial in persons with type 1 diabetes and others with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, but its role in the treatment of persons with type 2 diabetes not being treated with insulin has needed further study.

item.description:
Objectives: To critically evaluate the comparative effects of open or flexible family presence policies vs. restricted or traditional family presence policies on the occurrence of delirium and other major outcomes among adult patients admitted to ICUs.

Data sources: We conducted a comprehensive electronic search of MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to November 21, 2025.

Study selection: We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing open or flexible vs. restricted ICU visiting policies in adult patients.

Data extraction: The primary outcome extracted was delirium occurrence. Secondary outcomes included the duration of invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), ICU length of stay, hospital-acquired infections, and ICU mortality.

Data synthesis: Thirteen RCTs comprising 3861 patients were included. Random-effects models showed that compared with restricted policies, open/flexible family presence reduced delirium occurrence (risk ratio [RR], 0.48; 95% CI, 0.29-0.81; low certainty) and IMV duration (mean difference [MD], -0.36 d; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.26 d; low certainty). Conclusions: Open/flexible ICU family presence may reduce delirium and shorten the duration of IMV slightly, without increasing infections or ICU mortality, although the certainty of evidence is low and heterogeneity remains substantial.

Objectives: To assess the prognostic value of the mean Lethality Risk Score (LRS), reflecting the toxicity of substances involved in an exposure, and to develop prediction models for complicated outcomes in ICU patients with acute intoxication.

Design: Multicenter prospective cohort study.

Setting: Seventy-eight ICUs in Europe, Australia, and the Eastern Mediterranean (2020-2023).

Patients: A total of 2265 adult patients were admitted to the ICU with acute intoxication as the main reason for admission for at least 4 hours.

Measurements and main results: The primary outcome was defined as ICU complications or death (22.5%). Clinical data were collected in an electronic capture system. We developed two prediction models: one incorporating laboratory variables ("Laboratory Model"), and one including the mean LRS ("Expo Model"). The mean LRS was calculated as the average of the individual LRS values assigned to the toxicants involved in the exposure. Key predictors were age, severity at presentation, systolic blood pressure, Glasgow Coma Scale score, and hospital type. The mean LRS remained significant only when laboratory variables were not considered. Design: Nationwide retrospective cohort study using 2021-2023 Medicare claims linked to the American Hospital Association Annual Survey Database (AHAASD).

Setting: U.S. acute care hospitals.

Patients: Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries with ICU hospitalizations between 2022 and 2023.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: TCC capability was identified by AHAASD reporting and/or the presence of five or more TCC claims annually. The primary outcome was interhospital ICU transfer. Objectives: To describe ventilatory management in neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients and determine whether specific ventilator settings are associated with development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and mortality in neurocritical care patients. The primary endpoint was a diagnosis of ARDS after initiation of invasive ventilation; one secondary endpoint was ICU mortality.

Data sources: Post hoc pooled analysis of harmonized individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies combined into the PRIME database.

Study selection: PRIME is a harmonized pooled database comprising individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies on ventilatory management in critically ill patients: "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS" (PRoVENT), "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries" (PRoVENT-iMiC), and "Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes" (ENIO). We excluded patients with ARDS at the start of ventilation.

Data extraction: Demographic and clinical characteristics, ventilator settings, respiratory variables, arterial blood gas values, and clinical outcomes were extracted from the harmonized PRIME database. Derived ventilation parameters included tidal volume normalized to predicted body weight, driving pressure, respiratory system compliance, mechanical power, ventilatory ratio, and Pao2/Fio2 ratio.

Data synthesis: This analysis included 3848 patients, including 1702 neurocritical care and 1920 non-neurocritical care patients. Based on recorded ventilatory variables, neurocritical care patients received lower median tidal volumes (Vts), positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. They had lower median driving pressure (ΔP), mechanical power (MP) of ventilation, and ventilatory ratio, as well as higher respiratory system compliance compared with non-neurocritical care patients. These differences were consistently observed at both assessed time points. ARDS was diagnosed more frequently in neurocritical care patients than in non-neurocritical care patients (8.7% vs. 3.9%; p < 0.001), while ICU mortality was lower (14.3% vs. 22.8%; p < 0.001). Among neurocritical care patients, those who developed ARDS were ventilated with lower median Vt and higher Fio2 and had higher median ΔP and MP. Vt normalized for predicted body weight in neurocritical care patients was independently associated with the development of ARDS.

Conclusions: In this cohort, ventilatory management at the initial and 48-hour assessments differed between neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients, particularly with respect to key ventilator settings like Vt, positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. In neurocritical care patients, ARDS was more often diagnosed than in non-neurocritical care patients.

item.description:
Background: Airway secretion retention is common in patients with acute respiratory failure (ARF), particularly in those requiring noninvasive respiratory support (NIRS). High-frequency chest wall oscillation (HFCWO) may improve airway clearance but critical care evidence remains limited.

Research question: Does adding HFCWO to standard care improve clinical outcomes in patients with bronchial hypersecretion and ARF requiring NIRS?

Study design and methods: We conducted a single-center randomized controlled trial in a RICU. Patients with ARF requiring NIRS, including high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) and/or noninvasive ventilation (NIV), bronchial hypersecretion, and ineffective cough (peak cough expiratory flow <270 L/min) were randomized 1:1 to HFCWO plus standard care or standard care alone. The primary endpoint was therapeutic bronchoscopy. Secondary endpoints included hospital length of stay (LOS), RICU-LOS, NIRS duration, endotracheal intubation and mortality. Outcomes were analyzed using unadjusted and adjusted models accounting for age, sex, and main cause of hospitalization.

Results: Eighty-eight patients were enrolled (44 HFCWO, 44 control), with comparable baseline characteristics. item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Resuscitation training with school children - Analysis of factors affecting chest compression quality
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Early bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) improves survival after sudden cardiac arrest, but bystander CPR rates remain low. International guidelines therefore recommend CPR training during childhood. This study evaluated CPR performance in children aged 8-13 years and assessed determinants of chest compression quality.

Methods: In this observational cross-sectional study (2019-2022), 784 schoolchildren aged 8-13 years completed a standardized 90-min CPR training session. Anthropometric data and CPR quality parameters were recorded using Resusci Anne QCPR Torso manikins (Laerdal Medical AS, Starvanger, Norway) and SimPad Plus SkillReporter systems (Laerdal Medical AS, Starvanger, Norway). Associations were analyzed using multivariate statistics.

Results: A total of 784 children (mean age 11 ± 1 years) were included. Two minutes of chest compressions were completed by 93% of children. Mean compression depth was 40.0 ± 9.9 mm and correlated with weight (r = 0.663), height (r = 0.623), and age (r = 0,544; all p < .001). In multivariable analysis, these factors explained 50% of variance (R2 = 0.50, p < .001). Mean compression rate (115 ± 8/min) was higher in younger children and became more consistent with increasing age (ß = -0.119, p = .02). Correct hand positioning was achieved almost universally (median 100%).

Conclusion: A tailored and focused CPR training is feasible and effective in children aged 8-13 years but higher body weight improves compression depth, older age improves compression, while correct hand position is largely independent of these variables.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Acute hemorrhagic shock from vaginal laceration during intercourse requiring operative management
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Vaginal laceration during consensual intercourse is a rare cause of acute vaginal bleeding. Most coital injuries are minor, although may result in acute hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability. A 30-year-old G3P2012 otherwise healthy woman presented to the emergency department (ED) with acute vaginal bleeding immediately during consensual intercourse. She was initially well-appearing then developed hemorrhagic shock in the ED from ongoing vaginal exsanguination. The bleeding source could not be visualized on speculum examination. She was resuscitated with tranexamic acid, crystalloid, and two units of unmatched whole blood and taken emergently to the operating room. Examination under anesthesia after evacuation identified a horizontal posterior vaginal wall laceration. The laceration was repaired transvaginally with hemostasis, and the patient recovered uneventfully. A vaginal laceration during intercourse may cause acute life-threatening hemorrhage. Bleeding is often occult on speculum examinations although may progress rapidly to shock. Emergency clinicians should exclude pregnancy, initiate early resuscitation, and urgently consult gynecology for examination under anesthesia and repair when indicated.

item.title: J Emerg Med: Signs of Life and Clinical Outcomes in Patients With Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Multicenter Observational Study
item.description:
Background: The prognostic value of individual signs of life (SOLs) remains unclear in patients experiencing traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (t-OHCA).

Objectives: To describe clinical outcomes among patients with t-OHCA by the presence of each SOL at the scene.

Methods: Data from the SOS-KANTO 2017 study, a multicenter prospective registry of OHCA cases treated between 2019 and 2021, were retrospectively analyzed. Adult patients diagnosed with t-OHCA were included, excluding those with a palpable pulse upon emergency medical service (EMS) arrival. Patients were categorized into eight subgroups based on the presence of three SOLs at the scene-the pupillary light reflex, spontaneous respiration, and cardiac electrical activity - and descriptive analyses were performed. The primary outcome was survival beyond the emergency department (ED).

Results: Of the 462 patients included in the analysis, two (0.4%) exhibited all three SOLs, and 18 (3.9%) exhibited two SOLs; in the latter group, two demonstrated cardiac activity and a pupillary reflex, and 16 had cardiac activity and spontaneous respiration. Among the 124 patients (26.8%) with only one SOL, 117 had cardiac activity, three showed a pupillary reflex, and four exhibited spontaneous respiration. No SOLs were observed in 318 patients (68.8%). Overall, 22 patients (4.8%) survived beyond the ED. The highest survival rate was observed in the subgroup with both cardiac activity and spontaneous respiration (4/16; 25%), followed by the subgroup with cardiac activity alone (10/117; 8.5%).

Conclusions: Among the t-OHCA patients, survival beyond the ED was observed more frequently in those with cardiac electrical activity at the scene.

item.title: J Emerg Med: Efficacy of Inhaled Methoxyflurane for Acute Trauma Pain Management: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
item.description:
Background: Acute traumatic pain is common in emergency settings and inadequate analgesia can worsen physiological, psychological, and functional outcomes.

Study objectives: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy, onset of action, safety, and clinical practicality of inhaled methoxyflurane compared with control analgesic treatments for acute trauma-related pain.

Methods: Four databases were searched from inception through February 2026. Randomized controlled trials evaluating inhaled methoxyflurane for acute traumatic pain were eligible. Outcomes included visual analogue scale and numerical rating scale pain scores, rescue analgesia, time to first pain relief, and adverse events (AEs). Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and RevMan was used for quantitative synthesis.

Results: Seven studies involving 1585 participants were analyzed. Methoxyflurane significantly reduced the time to first pain relief compared with controls (mean difference -5.93 min, 95% confidence interval [CI] -6.86 to -5.00, p < 0.00001, I2 = 0%). Pain intensity also favored methoxyflurane at 5, 10, 15, and 20 min. Methoxyflurane also significantly reduced the need for rescue analgesia (risk ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.18-0.90, p = 0.03). Overall AEs were comparable, but dizziness, drowsiness, and cough were more frequent with methoxyflurane.

Conclusion: Inhaled methoxyflurane provides rapid and effective analgesia for acute traumatic pain and may reduce rescue analgesia needs. Further high-quality randomized trials are needed to clarify comparative effectiveness across trauma populations and emergency care settings.

item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a medical condition that is present in approximately 2.5% of adults worldwide and manifests in a variety of different ways across the lifespan. Adults with ADHD often have coexisting psychiatric disorders such as anxiety, mood, sleep, substance use, and personality disorders and are at increased risk for coexisting somatic conditions such as obesity, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, and immune and inflammatory conditions. Hence, such adults may be seen by clinicians providing care for a wide range of psychiatric and somatic conditions. Nevertheless, ADHD remains unrecognized and undiagnosed in many persons. Assessment requires interviewing of the patient for core ADHD symptoms, coexisting conditions, and their functional effects, which can be facilitated by using standardized rating scales. Key components of treatment are psychoeducation and psychostimulant or nonstimulant medication, mostly in combination with psychosocial interventions and lifestyle guidance.
