item.title: N Engl J Med: Long-Acting HIV Therapy in African Adults with Adherence Challenges
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: In eastern and southern Africa, approximately 1 million people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and receiving oral therapy do not have viral suppression because of adherence challenges.

Methods: We conducted a phase 3b, open-label, randomized trial to compare long-acting injectable cabotegravir plus rilpivirine with oral dolutegravir-based therapy among adults with virally suppressed HIV type 1 (viral load, <200 copies per milliliter) and suboptimal adherence or care engagement. The participants were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive intramuscular injections of cabotegravir (600 mg) plus rilpivirine (900 mg) every 8 weeks, with the first two injection visits occurring 4 weeks apart, or to continue daily oral dolutegravir-based therapy; baseline drug-resistance testing was not performed. The primary end point was a viral load of less than 50 copies per milliliter at week 48; noninferiority was assessed with a margin of -10 percentage points. Confirmed virologic failure (two consecutive viral loads of ≥200 copies per milliliter) was a key secondary end point.

Results: A total of 540 participants were enrolled across seven sites in Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda; 537 were included in the primary analysis. At 48 weeks, 244 of 268 participants (91.0%) in the long-acting-therapy group had a viral load of less than 50 copies per milliliter, as compared with 240 of 269 participants (89.2%) in the oral-therapy group (risk difference, 1.9 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -3.1 to 6.9), which met the criterion for noninferiority. The results of a per-protocol analysis were consistent with those of the primary analysis. Confirmed virologic failure occurred in 5 participants (1.9%) in the long-acting-therapy group and in no participants in the oral-therapy group (risk difference, 1.9 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.3 to 3.5). Serious adverse events were reported in 11 of 271 participants (4.1%) who received long-acting therapy and in 8 of 269 participants (3.0%) who received oral therapy (risk difference, 1.1 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.1 to 4.2).

Conclusions: Among persons with HIV in Africa who have adherence challenges, long-acting cabotegravir plus rilpivirine was noninferior to oral dolutegravir-based therapy for maintaining a viral load of less than 50 copies per milliliter. item.description:
Background: Monoclonal antibodies targeting the interleukin-23 pathway are effective in treating inflammatory bowel disease. However, these therapies must be administered intravenously or by subcutaneous injection.

Methods: We conducted a phase 2b, double-blind, randomized trial of oral icotrokinra, a peptide that blocks the interleukin-23 receptor, in adults with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis. Participants were assigned to receive icotrokinra at a once-daily dose of 400 mg, 200 mg, or 100 mg or placebo. The primary end point was clinical response at week 12. Secondary end points included clinical remission, remission of symptoms, and endoscopic improvement at week 12.

Results: A total of 252 participants underwent randomization: 63 were assigned to the 400-mg group, 62 to the 200-mg group, 64 to the 100-mg group, and 63 to the placebo group. All the doses of icotrokinra were superior to placebo with respect to a clinical response at week 12, which occurred in 63% of the participants in the 400-mg group, 58% in the 200-mg group, and 55% in the 100-mg group, as compared with 27% in the placebo group (P<0.001 for all comparisons with placebo). The percentage of participants with clinical remission at week 12 was also significantly higher in the 400-mg group than in the placebo group (30% vs. 11%, P = 0.006), as were the percentage of participants with symptomatic remission (46% vs. 19%, P<0.001) and the percentage of participants with endoscopic improvement (37% vs. 14%, P = 0.002). Clinical remission at week 12 occurred in 24% of the participants in the 200-mg group (P = 0.054 for the comparison with placebo); in accordance with the fixed-sequence testing procedure to account for multiple comparisons, no further formal testing of secondary end points was conducted. Through week 28, the percentage of participants with adverse events was 60% in the 400-mg group, 66% in the 200-mg group, 66% in the 100-mg group, and 62% in the placebo group. For serious adverse events, the percentages were 2%, 5%, 0%, and 10%, respectively.

Conclusions: Among participants with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, a clinical response at week 12 was significantly more common with once-daily oral icotrokinra at each of three tested doses than with placebo. item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: The outcome of Philadelphia-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph-positive ALL) has greatly improved with the use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immunotherapy.

Methods: In this trial, we randomly assigned adult patients with Ph-positive ALL in a 2:1 ratio to receive ponatinib plus blinatumomab (intervention group) or imatinib plus chemotherapy (control group) as frontline treatment. A crossover to the intervention group was allowed for patients with persistence or reappearance of measurable residual disease in the control group. The primary end point was event-free survival.

Results: A total of 236 patients underwent randomization: 158 to the intervention group and 78 to the control group. The median age of the patients was 55 years (range, 24 to 82). At a median follow-up of 23.7 months, the estimated 24-month event-free survival was 86% in the intervention group and 67% in the control group (P<0.001). Survival with no measurable residual disease was 68% and 42%, respectively. At the end of induction, a complete hematologic response was observed in 94% of the patients in the intervention group and in 79% of those in the control group. After blinatumomab consolidation, a molecular response was observed in 71% and 49% of the patients, respectively. After crossover to the intervention group, 20 of 31 patients (64%) had a molecular response. Overall survival was 90% in the intervention group and 85% in the control group. The cumulative incidence of relapse was 5% and 13%, respectively. As of this report, only 19% of the patients in the intervention group had undergone hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation after having had a first complete hematologic response.

Conclusions: In this phase 3 trial, a frontline chemotherapy-free targeted and immunotherapeutic approach was superior to the use of imatinib and chemotherapy. (Funded by Associazione Italiana per la Ricerca sul Cancro and others; GIMEMA ALL2820 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04722848.).

Importance: States may join the US Department of Agriculture Direct Certification with Medicaid (DCM) program, allowing schools to use Medicaid participation to automatically qualify students for free and reduced-price school meals (F/RP). DCM also informs the Identified Student Percentage (ISP), which determines eligibility for the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP). Pre-COVID-19 evaluations found mixed associations between DCM and school meal participation. Pandemic-era policies included free meals for all students, which has ended in most states. Therefore, a postpandemic evaluation of DCM is warranted.

Objective: To examine the association of Maryland's DCM implementation in the 2022-2023 school year (SY22-23) with ISP, CEP eligibility and enrollment, and school lunch participation.

Design, setting, and participants: In this cohort study, publicly available school-level data were used to examine annual ISP, CEP participation, and school lunch participation among public schools in Maryland. A school-level fixed effects model evaluated changes in school lunch participation before (SY18-19 and SY19-20) and after (SY22-23 and SY23-24) DCM implementation among non-CEP schools. A 2-way fixed effects model tested the association between CEP enrollment and school lunch participation among schools newly eligible for CEP due to DCM. Data analyses were conducted from July to December 2025.

Exposure: DCM implementation.

Main outcomes and measures: ISP, CEP eligibility and enrollment, and school lunch participation.

Results: Among 1252 schools, 856 (68.4%) were elementary, 221 (17.7%) were middle, and 175 (14.0%) were high schools; 734 (58.6%) were suburban, 258 (20.6%) were located in rural or small towns, and 260 (20.8%) were urban. item.description:
Importance: Although US health care organizations are attempting to improve physician retention, national data indicate that physician turnover is increasing. There are minimal data on the associations between physicians' assessment of their immediate supervisor and alignment of individual and organizational values and objective turnover.

Objective: To evaluate the association between individual responses from physician surveys evaluating named immediate supervisor and alignment of individual and organizational values with objective turnover during the following 2 years.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study included practicing physicians completing organizational surveys at a large, academic medical center between October 3, 2016, and May 1, 2024. Standardized instruments were used to assess leader behavior, alignment of individual and organizational values, burnout, and professional fulfillment at 5 survey time points. Individual survey responses were paired with human resources records on objective turnover.

Exposure: The 9-item Mayo Clinic Leadership Impact Index, Stanford Values Alignment Scale, Stanford Professional Fulfillment Index, and a measure of self-reported intent to leave within the next 2 years were administered.

Main outcomes and measures: Objective turnover was determined from human resource records. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to evaluate the association of leader behavior and alignment of individual and organizational values with turnover, adjusting for age, sex, survey year, and occupational well-being measures associated with turnover (ie, burnout and professional fulfillment).

Results: In aggregate, 7351 survey responses from 3124 unique physicians (1528 [48.9%] female) paired with 2-year objective turnover were available. The participation rate exceeded 50% in all survey years (2016: 1281 of 2392 [53.6%]; 2019: 1285 of 1924 [66.8%]; 2020: 1479 of 1909 [77.5%]; 2022: 1553 of 2251 [69.0%]; 2024: 1654 of 2498 [66.2%]) Each 1-point higher score (range, 0-10) for leader behavior (hazard ratio [HR], 0.89 [95% CI, 0.85-0.93]; P < .001) and values alignment (HR, 0.90 [95% CI, 0.86-0.94]; P < .001) was associated with decreased objective 2-year turnover. After adjusting for age, sex, survey year, values alignment, occupational burnout, and professional fulfillment, each 1-point difference in leadership behavior score (HR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.83-0.94]; P < .001) remained associated with objective 2-year turnover. The association between values alignment and 2-year objective turnover was no longer present in these analyses. On paired individual-level data from physicians completing consecutive surveys and adjusting for baseline score, each 1-point increase in leader behavior (HR, 0.82 [95% CI, 0.76-0.90]; P < .001) and values alignment (HR, 0.86 [95% CI, 0.79-0.93]; P < .001) score between surveys was associated with reduced turnover following the second survey. On multivariable analysis adjusting for age, sex, and survey year, respondents indicating moderate (HR, 3.22 [95% CI, 2.41-4.31]) or likely to definite intent to leave (HR, 8.58 [95% CI, 6.43-11.44]; P < .001) were at higher risk of objective 2-year turnover.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, physician evaluation of immediate supervisor behavior and alignment between individual and organizational values on organizational surveys were associated with subsequent objective turnover. These findings suggest that organizations seeking to promote physician retention should conduct leadership assessments, attend to leadership development, and foster values alignment with their physicians.

item.description:
Importance: US federal reporting changes in 2025 removed sexual orientation and gender identity (SOGI) measures from health-center reporting, raising concerns about equity surveillance.

Objective: To quantify how incomplete or absent SOGI data are associated with detection of disparities in documented HIV preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) orders.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study used electronic health record data from a large safety-net health system in Southern California. Data were from patients 18 years or older registered as of October 28, 2025, with documented PrEP orders from January 2, 2019, through October 27, 2025. Registration dates were unavailable, precluding common follow-up. Three surveillance scenarios were assessed: complete SOGI, sex assigned at birth (SAAB) only, and joint SOGI missingness from 0% to 90%. Adults with classifiable SAAB, sexual orientation, and gender identity were included.

Exposures: Complete, unavailable, or partially missing SOGI data.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was any documented PrEP order. Logistic regression models adjusted for age and race and ethnicity, with interactions of sexual orientation or gender identity with SAAB. Marginally standardized probabilities and adjusted percentage-point differences were estimated within SAAB strata. Each nonzero missing level included 250 simulations to assess the magnitude, precision, and statistical detectability of each difference.

A total of 1406 patients (0.9%) had a documented PrEP order. Neither difference was significant among patients assigned female at birth. Under SAAB-only surveillance, only a difference between male and female SAAB was measurable (1.4 pp; 95% CI, 1.3-1.5 pp; P < .001), whereas SOGI-specific differences were not estimable. item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Multi-Institutional Data for Faculty Well-Being Improvements Within and Across Medical Schools
item.description:
Importance: Burnout, engagement, and satisfaction vary in prevalence and correlate with organizational performance in US medical colleges. Large-scale improvements have been elusive.

Objective: To quantify rates of well-being and its organizational correlates so to help identify opportunities for shared learning and focus well-being interventions across and within medical schools.

Design, setting, and participants: In this cross-sectional study, 28 US medical schools accredited by the Liaison Committee on Medical Education were surveyed from January 26, 2021, through June 3, 2024. Of 28 919 eligible faculty, 16 994 participated (58.8%; range, 21% to 92%).

Exposure: The Association of American Medical Colleges' StandPoint Faculty Engagement Survey.

Main outcomes and measures: The psychological states of burnout, satisfaction, and organizational commitment as a proxy for engagement and their antecedents. Heterogeneity beyond chance was quantified in the rates across and within schools using the I2 statistic. Positive deviants, or bright spots, were identified as those schools and departments whose confidence intervals did not include the group mean rate. Regression analyses assessed the factors contributing to the success of the positive deviants.

Results: Across 15 404 respondents (9093 [53.5%] identified as men), a pooled 32% reported burnout. Across schools, there was substantial heterogeneity in rates beyond chance of burnout (13%-41%; I2 = 75%), commitment (pooled 80% [range, 74%-95%]; I2 = 82%), and satisfaction (pooled 77% [range, 62%-86%]; I2 = 80%). Few departments (67 of 502 [13.3%]) had a favorable rate of both commitment and burnout. For rates of burnout at the department level, 32% of the variance was explained by the rates of burnout of their school and discipline; the rates of autonomy, purpose, and belonging; and gender and age. The burnout of individuals was explained by the mean burnout score of one's department (R2 = 4%), with no contribution by the school or discipline. When combined with the factors contributing to departmental variation, 24% of the variance in burnout across individuals was explained.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study, the substantial heterogeneity beyond chance and identification of positive deviants (bright spots) support the opportunity for learning health systems and learning communities across and within schools and professional societies to identify positive deviant departments or schools and share details of implementing existing successful practices for promoting well-being. Both burnout and engagement should be monitored within and across medical schools, as these measures may not converge.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Cultural Engagement and Hospital-Treated Mental Disorders in Older Adults
item.description:
Importance: Cultural engagement is associated longitudinally with better mental health and reduced depression incidence, but evidence has largely relied on self-reported symptoms and diagnoses, leaving uncertainty about clinically recorded disorders, and residual confounding remains a concern.

Objective: To examine whether cultural engagement is associated with incident hospital-treated mental disorders.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective cohort study included adults aged 50 years and older from the English Longitudinal Study of Aging (wave 4, May 2008 to July 2009), with follow-up through March 2024. Data were analyzed from November 2025 to March 2026.

Exposures: Frequency of engagement with any of the receptive arts activities (ie, watching or consuming performances or exhibitions) was categorized as never, infrequent (less than once a year up to once or twice a year), or frequent (every few months up to monthly or more).

Main outcomes and measures: Participant records were linked to diagnostic codes in Hospital Episode Statistics and mortality records with follow-up of up to 20 years. The primary outcomes were mental disorders overall and 4 main mental disorders (dementia, substance misuse, mood disorders, and neurotic disorders). Cox proportional hazard regression models were used to estimate the hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs, with a false discovery rate (FDR) approach for significance. To further probe causality, eye disease, ear disease, and traumatic brain injury-which share similar sociodemographic profiles to mental disorders-were prespecified as negative control outcomes.

Results: This study included 8274 adults (mean [SD] age, 65.4 [9.6] years; 4672 female [55.2%]). After fully adjusting for sociodemographic, lifestyle, and social factors and multiple testing, frequent cultural engagement was associated with lower risk of any mental disorders (HR, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.62-0.82; PFDR < .001), dementia (HR, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.56-0.89; FDR-adjusted P = .01), substance misuse (HR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.95; FDR-adjusted P = .04), and mood disorders (HR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.56-0.95; FDR-adjusted P = .04), but not neurotic disorders. Associations persisted after excluding early incident cases and adjusting for baseline depressive symptoms and cognition and showed robustness to unmeasured confounders. Cultural engagement was not associated with any negative control outcomes.

Conclusions and relevance: In this nationally representative cohort of older adults, cultural engagement was associated with a lower hazard of subsequent hospital-treated mental disorders, with particularly consistent associations for dementia, substance misuse, and mood disorders. These findings provide triangulated statistical data to suggest that cultural engagement is associated with reduced risk of several clinically recorded mental disorders and support further testing of cultural engagement as a population mental health strategy.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Uptake and Inequalities in Exercise-Based Cardiac Rehabilitation After Decentralization
item.description:
Importance: Despite clinical benefits and guideline recommendations, uptake of exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation (CR) following coronary artery disease remains suboptimal, with barriers including transportation issues, travel distance, and geographic location. To overcome these barriers, decentralization strategies that move health care to local settings have been developed across several countries.

Objective: To determine whether CR uptake improved following decentralization, and whether geographic and social inequalities were reduced.

Design, setting, and participants: This register-based cohort study used data from 2013 to 2022, with data analysis performed from April to August 2025. This population-based study was conducted within 21 Danish municipalities. All participants were patients aged 30 years or older discharged alive after acute myocardial infarction, percutaneous coronary intervention, or coronary artery bypass grafting. Patients were identified in the Danish National Patient Register. Patients were excluded if they had a previous diagnosis or procedure or did not reside within the study area.

Exposures: Travel distance from home to nearest CR facility and educational level.

Main outcomes and measures: Uptake (attending at least 1 training session within 180 days from discharge) was analyzed using modified Poisson regression to quantify differences in proportions before and after decentralization with adjustment for relevant covariates.

Results: A total of 19 375 patients were eligible for the study, and 295 patients with missing information on exposures or covariates were excluded. Among the included 19 080 patients, 13 355 (70.0%) were male, and 10 868 (57.0%) were aged 60 to 79 years. The median (IQR) travel distance was reduced from 15.1 (5.9-25.7) km to 7.2 (2.8-14.8) km after decentralization, and uptake increased by 16% (risk ratio [RR], 1.16; 95% CI, 1.12-1.19). Among the 20% of patients with the longest travel distance, uptake increased by 45% (RR, 1.45; 95% CI, 1.33-1.58), and geographic inequality was significantly reduced. Among patients with short education, uptake increased by 27% (RR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.20-1.35), and social inequality was significantly reduced.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of 19 080 patients, there was increased uptake of CR after decentralization to primary care, accompanied by significant reductions in geographic and social inequalities. The findings support decentralized delivery of CR as a feasible and equitable model, but ongoing monitoring of quality and safety remains essential.

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: Prehospital Care of Older Adults Following Perceived Low-Acuity Falls and Related "Lift Assist" Encounters: An NAEMSP Position Statement and Resource Document
item.description:
Older adults who present as low-acuity falls requiring mobilization assistance, commonly referred to as a "lift assist", represent a common reason for EMS activation. These encounters often involve underlying medical conditions or injuries that are not immediately apparent, and missed or delayed diagnosis is associated with adverse outcomes. At the same time, some patients are transported to the emergency department when it is not necessary, exposing them to potential harms and contributing to increased healthcare utilization. These encounters are therefore complex clinical presentations and represent important opportunities for thorough assessment and higher-order clinical decision making, supported by systems that enable appropriate disposition and follow-up. However, there is a system-level bias, beginning in initial education and reinforced through dispatch, policy, and protocol, that frames these encounters as uniformly low-acuity, non-medical, minor traumas leading to underassessment and limiting clinical decision-making. Therefore, NAEMSP recommends:EMS systems should recognize calls for falls or "lift assists" as patient encounters that warrant an assessment, including evaluation for underlying medical causes, traumatic injuries, and safety, and frame these encounters as opportunities for higher-order clinical decision-making within the broader context of geriatric syndromes rather than isolated low-acuity events.EMS systems should support transport decisions based on a thorough assessment and patient-centered discussion, recognizing that not all patients require ED transport and that safe alternatives may include non-transport or referral to appropriate follow-up pathways.EMS systems should track the assessment of patients encountered during "lift assist" responses and older adults following perceived low acuity falls as a system-level quality measure to monitor performance and drive improvement.Policymakers and payers should implement sustainable reimbursement structures that support EMS assessment and care even when transport does not occur.

item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: The preferred method of renal-replacement therapy for acute kidney injury in critically ill patients remains uncertain.

Methods: In this multicenter, open-label, noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned critically ill adults with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy to undergo intermittent hemodialysis or continuous renal-replacement therapy as the initial treatment. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event - defined as death, dependence on renal-replacement therapy, or a serum creatinine concentration more than 25% above the baseline value - by day 90.

Results: The trial was stopped early after sequential interim analyses showed a sustained signal of higher mortality with intermittent hemodialysis than with continuous renal-replacement therapy. A total of 554 patients underwent randomization, with 272 patients assigned to undergo intermittent hemodialysis and 282 to undergo continuous renal-replacement therapy; 535 patients (260 in the intermittent group and 275 in the continuous group) were included in the intention-to-treat population. A major adverse kidney event occurred by day 90 in 203 patients (78.1%) in the intermittent group and in 197 patients (71.6%) in the continuous group (adjusted absolute risk difference, 6.28 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.22 to 13.79). Death by day 90 occurred in 164 patients (63.1%) and in 147 patients (53.5%), respectively. Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates at day 90 were 63.3% and 53.6% (hazard ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.63). The most common complication potentially related to acute kidney injury or renal-replacement therapy was hypotension, which occurred in 179 patients (68.8%) in the intermittent group and in 183 patients (66.5%) in the continuous group.

Conclusions: Among critically ill patients with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy, intermittent hemodialysis as the initial treatment approach was not shown to be noninferior to continuous renal-replacement therapy with respect to major adverse kidney events by day 90 and was associated with higher mortality. item.title: JAMA: Isoflurane-Based Inhaled Sedation in Mechanically Ventilated Adults With Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: The SAVE-ICU Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Rigorous evidence for inhaled sedation using isoflurane in mechanically ventilated patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) is limited.

Objective: To evaluate whether an inhaled sedation strategy lowers hospital mortality compared with usual care intravenous sedation strategy in mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF.

Design, setting, and participants: Pragmatic, effectiveness, open-label, superiority, randomized clinical trial in 14 intensive care units (ICUs) in Canada. Adults (≥18 years) receiving sedation for less than 72 hours and receiving mechanical ventilation for AHRF from non-COVID respiratory failure (ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen [Pao2] to fraction of inspired oxygen [Fio2] <300 mm Hg) or COVID-19 were enrolled between September 2020 and March 2025 with follow-up through June 2025.

Intervention: Patients were randomized to an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed or to a usual intravenous sedation care strategy. Sedatives were titrated to achieve the desired target sedation score guided by clinical teams and continued until extubation or death.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcome was all-cause hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU- and ventilator-free days at day 30; hospital-free days at day 60; use of refractory hypoxemia adjunctive therapies; delirium- and coma-free days at day 14; and quality-of-life and disability scores at 3 months.

Results: Of 786 patients randomized, 780 were included in the primary analysis (mean age, 61.1 years; 34.0% female; 73.7% non-COVID AHRF, mean Pao2:Fio2 ratio, 152.6 mm Hg); 385 in the inhaled sedation and 395 in the intravenous sedation groups. In the inhaled sedation group, 49.9% to 55.4% of patients received concomitant intravenous sedation on any day during the first 14 days after randomization. At hospital discharge, 161 of 379 patients (42.5%) in the inhaled sedation group had died, compared with 171 of 390 patients (43.8%) in the intravenous sedation group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.84 to 1.14]; P = .85). There was no effect modification in prespecified subgroup analyses for age, sex, and COVID-19 status. ICU-, ventilator-, and hospital-free days were similar between groups. The inhaled sedation group received more adjunctive therapies for hypoxemia (239 [63.9%] vs 214 [55.0%]; between-group difference, 8.89% [95% CI, 1.95% to 15.83%]) and had fewer delirium- and coma-free days (between-group difference, -0.95 [95% CI, -1.69 to -0.22]). There was no difference in quality-of-life and disability scores between groups.

Conclusions and relevance: In mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF, an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed did not reduce hospital mortality compared with an intravenous sedation strategy.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Tools Measuring Health Literacy in Critically Ill Patients and Their Caregivers: A Scoping Review
item.description:
Objectives: Health literacy, the ability to understand and use health information, is important for critically ill patients and their caregivers in the neonatal ICU (NICU), PICU, and adult ICU to make informed decisions and navigate complex care. This review aimed to identify and summarize tools used to assess health literacy in critically ill patients or their caregivers.

Data sources: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycINFO through July 24, 2025.

Study selection: Included articles reported on tools to assess health literacy in critically ill patients or their caregivers. Two reviewers independently performed screening and data extraction.

Data extraction: Two independent reviewers extracted data in Covidence. Data items included study characteristics (country in which the study was conducted, study funding, study setting) and health literacy tool characteristics (tool user, types of questions in the tool, method of tool administration, if the tool was created by the study team, and if a full version was available in the publication).

Data synthesis: We included 92 articles describing 84 health literacy tools. Tools measured: 1) topic-specific clinical knowledge (e.g., organ donation, cardiopulmonary resuscitation; n = 24/84, 29%; NICU: n = 9; PICU: n = 1; ICU: n = 14); 2) ICU prognosis, diagnosis, and treatment (n = 23/84, 27%; NICU: 6; PICU: 3; ICU: n = 15); 3) neonatal and parenting (n = 13/84, 15%; all NICU); 4) general health literacy abilities (n = 11/84, 13%; NICU: n = 6; PICU: n = 2; ICU: n = 7); 5) information needs (n = 4/84, 5%; NICU: n = 1; PICU: n = 0; ICU: n = 3); 6) readiness for discharge (n = 3/84, 4%; all NICU); 7) decision-making (n = 3/84, 4%; all NICU); 8) health-related behaviors (n = 2/84, 2%; NICU: n = 1; ICU: n = 1); and 9) research participation (n = 1/84, 1%; NICU).

Conclusions: Although several health literacy tools exist, they often focus on individual knowledge of specific aspects of ICU care, with less attention to how understanding is produced within the clinical context through interactions among patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers. This may limit their ability to reflect how health literacy functions in critical illness. Assessment of health literacy requires pairing the appropriate tools with interaction-focused approaches to guide communication and support informed decision-making in ICU settings.

item.description:
Objectives: Evaluate the association between cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) ventilation rates and survival to hospital discharge, and identify novel ventilation targets.

Design: Multicenter prospective ancillary observational cohort study of the ICU-RESUS trial (NCT02837497).

Setting: A total of 18 ICUs from 10 U.S. clinical sites from October 2016 to March 2021.

Patients: Hospitalized children (≤ 18 yr) with endotracheal or tracheostomy tubes and evaluable intra-arrest end-tidal carbon dioxide data to calculate ventilation rate.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: Among 234 included events, 86 events (36.8%) had guideline-recommended (20-30 beats per min [bpm]) average ventilation rates during CPR. The association between guideline-recommended CPR ventilation rate and survival to hospital discharge was evaluated with Poisson regression using generalized estimating equations, controlling for a priori covariables (initial pulse status, immediate cause of arrest). We found no association between guideline-recommended ventilation rates and survival to hospital discharge (adjusted relative risk [aRR], 0.95; 95% CI, 0.75-1.21; p = 0.68). In exploratory analyses, novel age-stratified ventilation rates were identified using natural cubic splines and subsequently evaluated in multivariable models. We identified potential thresholds (< 8 yr, ≥ 26 bpm; ≥ 8 yr, < 26 bpm). For children younger than 8 years, average CPR ventilation rate greater than or equal to 26 bpm was associated with improved survival to hospital discharge compared with less than 26 bpm (aRR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.00-1.73; p = 0.048).

Conclusions: CPR ventilation rates in the currently recommended range (20-30 bpm) were not associated with survival in children with in-hospital cardiac arrest. In exploratory analyses in children younger than 8 years, higher ventilation rates (≥ 26 bpm) were associated with improved survival and warrant confirmation in future studies.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Association of Oliguria With Acute Kidney Injury, Chronic Kidney Disease, and Mortality: Determining the Optimal Threshold in Critically Ill Patients
item.description:
Objectives: Oliguria is a key prognostic indicator of acute kidney injury (AKI), yet the consensus definition (< 0.5 mL/kg/hr) is increasingly questioned. We aimed to determine thresholds of lowest mean diuresis (LMD) associated with AKI, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and mortality.

Design: Retrospective observational study.

Setting: Uppsala University Hospital ICU, Sweden.

Patients: A total of 4999 adults (≥ 18 yr) without preexisting CKD admitted to the ICU between 2017 and 2024.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: LMD was calculated over 3, 6, 12, and 24 hours (LMD3h-LMD24h). Generalized additive models were used, adjusting for Simplified Acute Physiology Score 3 estimated mortality ratio and gender. Outcomes were AKI within 7 days of LMD (Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes creatinine criteria), incident CKD after ICU discharge, and 90-day mortality. All LMD time frames were significantly associated with AKI, CKD, and death (p < 0.0001). Thresholds for AKI were 0.43, 0.41, 0.42, and 0.53 mL/kg/hr; for CKD, 0.21, 0.21, 0.31, and 0.43 mL/kg/hr; and for mortality 0.16, 0.18, 0.24, and 0.39 across LMD3h-LMD24h.

Conclusions: The risk of mortality or persistent kidney injury, reflected by incident CKD, increases at a lower urine output threshold than the current AKI definition. These findings support the idea of filtration deficit, urine output, and tissue injury as different dimensions of AKI and should influence future AKI definitions.

Mixed-effects logistic regression analyses were performed to evaluate the association between caregiver PICS-F and patient PICS. Ninety-four caregiver-patient dyads were analyzed. Caregivers were a median of 67 years old (55-79 yr old), 31 (33.0%) were male, and 41 (43.6%) were spouses. Patients were a median of 74 years old (69-82 yr old), and 54 (57.4%) were male. item.description:
Importance: The optimal vasopressor dose at which to initiate a second vasopressor in patients with septic shock is uncertain.

Objective: To compare the effects of hospital-level strategies initiating vasopressin infusion at a lower threshold vs a higher threshold on outcomes in patients with septic shock.

Design, setting, and participants: Cluster-randomized, cluster-crossover, pragmatic clinical strategy trial including adult patients receiving vasopressors for septic shock at 13 hospitals in Idaho and Utah from February 1, 2024, to July 31, 2025. The last day of follow-up for the primary outcome was February 17, 2026.

Intervention: Hospital-level implementation of septic shock management strategies recommending fixed-dose vasopressin initiation when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.1 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (lower-threshold strategy) or when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.4 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (higher-threshold strategy). Hospitals were randomized for the first month to an initial strategy (6 hospitals to the lower threshold vs 7 hospitals to the higher threshold) and then crossed over to the alternate strategy monthly thereafter.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome of 28-day mortality and the key secondary outcome of kidney replacement therapy-free days through day 28 were analyzed using multivariable generalized linear mixed-effects models, accounting for trial site and baseline patient characteristics.

Results: There were 3959 unique patients with septic shock (median age, 68 [IQR, 57 to 77] years; 1903 [48%] were female). Of the patients more likely to experience differential management under the tested hospital-level vasopressin dose strategies (maximum vasopressor dose ≥0.07 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent), 1034 of 1521 (68.0%) cared for under the lower-threshold strategy received vasopressin compared with 651 of 1526 (42.7%) cared for under the higher-threshold strategy. In the hospital-level strategy recommending a lower-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation, the maximum vasopressor dose received prior to vasopressin initiation was a median of 0.14 (IQR, 0.10 to 0.22) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent vs 0.34 (IQR, 0.16 to 0.42) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent in the hospital-level strategy recommending a higher-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation. Mortality at 28 days occurred in 628 of 1975 patients (31.8%) treated with the hospital-level strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower-dose threshold of other vasopressors vs 655 of 1984 patients (33.0%) treated with the higher-threshold strategy (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.87 to 1.06], P = .62; adjusted risk difference, -0.4 [95% CI, -2.7 to 1.3] percentage points). Patients in both strategies for vasopressin initiation had a median of 29 (IQR, -1 to 29) kidney replacement therapy-free days (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.91 to 1.14]).

Conclusions and relevance: In this large, pragmatic clinical trial comparing the effectiveness of 2 hospital-level strategies for second-line vasopressor management in septic shock, a strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower dose of other vasopressors did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with a strategy recommending vasopressin initiation at a higher dose of other vasopressors.

item.description:
Importance: International guidelines recommend dobutamine for management of septic shock and cardiac dysfunction with persistent hypoperfusion in adults based on very low-certainty evidence. Randomized trials are lacking on the effect of intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine vs norepinephrine on postoperative outcomes in patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control.

Objective: To determine whether intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine reduces acute kidney injury (AKI) within 7 postoperative days in patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control.

Design, setting, and participants: This randomized, open-label clinical trial in 39 tertiary hospitals in China enrolled adults with septic shock who were undergoing surgical source control between June 2024 and August 2025. Follow-up ended on November 15, 2025.

Intervention: Intraoperative, intravenous infusion of dobutamine (up to 5 µg/kg/min) combined with norepinephrine vs norepinephrine alone.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was new-onset AKI or worsening of preoperative AKI within 7 days after surgery, defined using Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. The 11 secondary outcomes included Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score on postoperative day 1 and urine output 1 hour post intervention.

Results: Among 584 patients (median [IQR] age, 67.5 [55.0-76.0] years; 192 [32.9%] females), new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days occurred in 22.8% (66/290) randomized to receive dobutamine plus norepinephrine vs 34.7% (102/294) randomized to receive norepinephrine alone (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 0.64 [95% CI, 0.49-0.83]). No significant differences were observed in 9 of the 11 secondary outcomes. Tachycardia (heart rate >100/min) occurred more frequently in patients receiving dobutamine and norepinephrine than norepinephrine alone.

Conclusions and relevance: Among adult patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control, intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine reduced the incidence of new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days compared with norepinephrine.

item.title: Acad Emerg Med: Conservative Versus Higher Oxygen Targets Post-Cardiac Arrest: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Trial Sequential Analysis
item.category: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine
item.description:
Background: Optimal oxygenation following return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) remains uncertain, as both hypoxemia and hyperoxemia risk secondary injury. We conducted an updated systematic review and meta-analysis comparing the efficacy of restrictive versus higher oxygenation targets.

Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis following the PRISMA 2020 protocol was carried out from database inception through June 2026. Only RCTs examining the impact of restrictive oxygenation versus higher oxygenation for adult CA patients undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation were included. Risks of bias and the quality of the evidence were evaluated using RoB 2 and GRADE tools. A random-effects model was used for data synthesis and presented the results in RR/MD.

Results: Eleven RCTs (12 reports) involving 4136 participants were included. Restrictive oxygenation showed no significant difference in all-cause mortality (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.88-1.06) or unfavorable neurological outcomes (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.88-1.04). Most subgroup analyses were non-significant, except for reduced mortality in the strict hypothermia subgroup (33°C-34°C), although TSA showed unstable evidence. No significant differences were observed in secondary outcomes. Restrictive oxygenation increased hypoxemia risk (RR 1.65) but improved ventilator-free days (MD 2.14).

Conclusion: There is no significant improvement in overall mortality, neurological outcome, or any other major clinical endpoint in adult CA patients with restrictive oxygen compared to higher oxygen therapy. Under current normothermia (36°C-37.5°C) protocols, the accumulated evidence trends toward futility for a restrictive approach, though the definitive information size has not yet been entirely accrued. Although restrictive levels could lead to an increased number of ventilator-free days, there will be an increased risk of hypoxemia.

item.title: Acad Emerg Med: Prevalence of Professional Interpreter Use in Emergency Departments: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
item.category: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine
item.description:
Background: Emergency departments (EDs) increasingly serve linguistically diverse populations. Professional interpretation improves care, yet its use remains variable. Quantifying the prevalence of use and understanding disparities can inform policies and interventions. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to estimate the prevalence of professional interpreter use in English-speaking EDs and compare use across patient populations and countries.

Methods: Eight databases were searched from inception to May 15, 2025. We screened full texts included in a prior scoping review to identify studies reporting the prevalence of professional interpreter use among patients requiring interpretation in English-speaking EDs. We pooled prevalence overall and stratified by population (adult vs. children) and country (United States vs. other), with 95% prediction intervals and confidence intervals (CIs). Meta-regression assessed associations between study year and prevalence. Risk of bias was evaluated using the JBI checklist for prevalence studies.

Results: Thirty-two studies spanning 1997-2025 involving 65,736 participants were included. Professional interpreters were used in 29% (CI, 20%, 38%) of encounters with patients requiring interpretation. Use was higher with children (49%; CI, 41%, 58%) than adults (16%; CI, 11%, 22%), and higher in the United States (33%; CI, 24%, 43%) than other countries (14%; CI, 4%, 30%). There was no significant association between study year and interpreter use (p = 0.38).

Conclusions: Despite known benefits, professional interpreter use in EDs remains low, particularly among adults and outside the United States. Addressing this gap will require coordinated efforts from clinicians, health system leaders, and policymakers to improve access to and accountability for language-concordant care in EDs.

item.title: JAMA: Fluid Therapy in Mechanically Ventilated Critically Ill Adult Patients
item.description:
Importance: Fluid therapy is ubiquitous in the intensive care unit (ICU) but carries risks, especially in mechanically ventilated patients. Contemporary global practice across dose, indication, and type is unknown.

Objective: To characterize ICU fluid practices in mechanically ventilated adults.

Design, setting, and participants: International prospective observational cohort study between April 2024 and July 2025, across 206 ICUs in 41 countries on 6 continents. Consecutive adult patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation within 3 days of ICU admission and ventilated 24 hours or more. Exclusion criteria were age younger than 16 years and transfer under mechanical ventilation from another ICU.

Exposures: Fluid volume, indication, and type after intubation.

Main outcomes and measures: Key measures included (1) total infused volume and daily fluid balance over 7 days after intubation; (2) the indication for fluid therapy over the first 3 days after intubation; (3) the proportion of total administered fluid volume attributable to each fluid type over the first 3 days after intubation.

Results: Among 2454 patients analyzed (median age, 63 years [IQR, 49-73 years]; 63.6% [1560] male), median daily fluid input peaked on day 1 at 3.0 L (IQR, 2.2-4.0 L) and declined to 2.6 L (IQR, 1.8-3.5 L) through day 6. Daily fluid balance (median, 0.9 L; IQR, 0.1-1.9 L on day 1) decreased to less than 0.3 L (IQR, -0.5 to 1.2 L) by day 3 and remained near-neutral through day 6. Maintenance and replacement fluids (to meet daily requirements and to correct ongoing losses; 31.9%) and creep fluids (to deliver medications and maintain catheter patency; 30.9%) were the primary indications, whereas resuscitation (to restore circulating blood volume; 16.0%) accounted for a smaller proportion. Isotonic balanced crystalloids (48.9%) and isotonic saline (0.9% sodium chloride) (27.0%) were common; colloids were rare (1.3%). Substantial between-site variation persisted after adjustment for case-mix.

Conclusions and relevance: In this prospective international cohort study, fluid therapy varied widely among mechanically ventilated critically ill patients, with maintenance and creep fluids-rather than resuscitation fluids-accounting for most total volume.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Shoulder anterior capsular (SHAC) block for analgesia in anterior shoulder dislocation: An emergency department case series
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Anterior shoulder dislocation is among the most common major joint dislocations presenting to the emergency department (ED) and is frequently managed with procedural sedation. Several analgesic and regional anesthesia strategies are available for shoulder reduction, each with distinct advantages and limitations. The Shoulder Anterior Capsular (SHAC) block is a superficial, ultrasound-guided interfascial plane technique that targets pericapsular nerve contributions to the glenohumeral joint via an anterior approach, offering a potentially motor-sparing and sedation-sparing alternative.

Case presentation: We present two cases of ED anterior shoulder dislocation managed with the SHAC block at a high-volume Level 1 trauma center. In the first case, a 60-year-old male with recurrent dislocation underwent successful reduction without procedural sedation, reporting it as his least painful reduction among multiple prior experiences. In the second case, a 94-year-old female with a complex fracture-dislocation in cervical spine precautions received the SHAC block as an analgesic adjunct; although procedural sedation was ultimately required, the patient required no intravenous analgesia during a subsequent 36-h observation period. In both cases, the block was performed by an emergency medicine intern under supervision by a Pain Medicine fellowship-trained attending physician, preserving the ability to conduct post-reduction axillary nerve assessment.

Conclusion: The SHAC block was technically feasible in two selected patients with anterior shoulder dislocation and provided variable analgesia. Further study is needed to evaluate its efficacy, safety, positioning requirements, reproducibility, and appropriate patient selection.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Associations between kratom (Mitragyna Speciosa) use and real-time anxiety and sadness: A 15-day ecological momentary assessment study
item.description:
Background: Kratom (Mitragyna Speciosa) is increasingly used in the U.S. for self-management of pain and mental health symptoms, yet its real-time effects on emotional distress remain poorly understood. We used ecological momentary assessment (EMA) to examine momentary associations of kratom use with anxiety and sadness.

Methods: A secondary analysis was conducted among 357 adult kratom consumers who adults who consume kratom completed a 15-day EMA protocol. Multilevel models assessed whether kratom use events occurring within the prior 180min were associated with momentary anxiety and sadness, and whether these associations were moderated by past 30-day use of prescribed anxiolytic or antidepressant medications.

Results: After adjusting for covariates, both single and multiple kratom use events in the previous 180min were associated with lower momentary anxiety compared to no use. For sadness, only single use events were significantly associated with lower scores. Past 30-day prescribed anxiolytic and antidepressant use did not significantly moderate these associations. Higher baseline anxiety and depressive symptoms were associated with greater momentary anxiety and sadness across the 15-day study period.

Conclusions: Kratom use was associated with small reductions in anxiety and, to a lesser extent, sadness in naturalistic settings. These associations were not influenced by past 30-day history of anxiolytic and antidepressant use. These results highlight kratom's potential role in real-time self-management of emotional distress while underscoring the need for randomized controlled trials and longitudinal studies to determine its clinical significance and long-term impact on mental health.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Digital and Coaching Interventions for Uptake of Cancer Genetic Testing: The MiGHT Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Germline genetic testing (GT) for hereditary cancer risk can inform cancer treatment, screening, and prevention, yet testing rates remain low. Alternative strategies are needed to improve facilitation of GT.

Objective: To compare 2 patient-level interventions to increase uptake of hereditary cancer GT against usual care.

Design, setting, and participants: The Michigan Genetic Hereditary Testing (MiGHT) randomized clinical trial analyzed self-reported GT outcome data from participants meeting clinical GT criteria between April 21, 2022, and November 21, 2025. Participants were adults (age ≥18 years) who met national criteria for genetic evaluation and had not previously completed germline GT recruited from oncology, primary care, and gastroenterology practices; research registries; and the general public in Michigan. Data were analyzed from April 30, 2025, to May 1, 2026.

Interventions: Participants were randomized to either telephone-based health coaching, a self-directed digital intervention, or usual care. Both interventions incorporated genetics education and motivational interviewing concepts.

Main outcomes and measures: GT uptake was assessed at 6- and 12-month time points. The primary outcome was completion of GT by 6 months. The effects of study group on GT uptake were evaluated using logistic regression, adjusting for cancer history, age, gender, and race.

Results: A total of 793 participants (median [IQR] age, 64 [51-71] years; 458 [57.8%] female) were randomized to health coaching (261 participants), the digital intervention (265 participants), or usual care (267 participants). Overall, 31 participants (4.9%) reported completing GT by the 6-month time point, and 76 participants (9.6%) underwent GT across the 12-month study period. Compared with usual care, participants in the digital intervention group had higher odds of completing GT by 6 months (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 3.88; 97.5% CI, 1.27-14.80), while those in the health coaching group had higher odds of completing GT by 12 months (AOR, 2.25; 97.5% CI, 1.11-4.77). Participants in the digital intervention group were more likely to express intention to test at 6 months (AOR, 2.36; 95% CI, 1.44-3.93), whereas those in the health coaching group had higher intention at both 6 (AOR, 2.99; 95% CI, 1.83-4.95) and 12 (AOR, 2.29; 95% CI 1.29-4.15) months compared with usual care.

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial of GT interventions, GT uptake was higher among participants who received the digital or health coaching interventions compared with usual care, although overall testing rates were low. These results underscore the importance of content delivery, motivational messaging, and alternative GT care models.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Trends in Violence Against Children in Australia
item.description:
Importance: Administrative data are commonly used to monitor multiple forms of violence against children, within and external to the family, yet different systems capture distinct thresholds of harm. Reliance on single data sources may obscure population-level trends.

Objective: To examine trends in multiple indicators of children's exposure to violence in Australia from 2014 to 2024 and to assess whether trends differ across police, health, and child protection data sources.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study used a time-trend analysis of Australian national administrative data spanning from 2014 to 2024. Data sources included national police-recorded assaults, hospitalizations, and child protection data from 3 Australian national agency databases. Participants were children aged 0 to 17 years, disaggregated by sex and age group. Analyses were conducted from January to April 2026.

Exposures: Year, modeled continuously.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcomes were annual rates per 100 000 population on police-recorded sexual assault, family and domestic violence (FDV)-related assault, hospitalizations for assault, and child maltreatment substantiations. Temporal trends were modeled using quasi-Poisson regression with population offsets, and average annual percentage changes were estimated. Turning points were assessed using Davies test and segmented regression.

Results: Annual population denominators ranged from 2.6 to 2.8 million girls and 2.7 to 3.0 million boys aged 0 to 17 years. Police-recorded sexual assault rates increased steadily among girls aged 0 to 9 years (2.8% per year; 95% CI, 2.0% to 3.6% per year) and those aged 10 to 17 years (4.2% per year; 95% CI, 3.4% to 5.0% per year). Among boys aged 10 to 17 years, rates accelerated sharply after 2021 (15.7% per year; 95% CI, 5.5% to 26.9% per year). FDV-related assault showed a similar trend, with stable to modest increases before 2021 followed by steep increases thereafter. Assault-related hospitalizations were generally stable, except for declines among boys aged 10 to 17 years (-1.4% per year; 95% CI, -2.7% to -0.1% per year). Overall child maltreatment substantiation remained stable, but declines were found for physical (-3.2% per year; 95% CI, -5.2% to -1.2% year) and sexual (-3.6% per year; 95% CI, -5.2% to -2.0% per year) abuse, alongside an increase in emotional abuse substantiations to 2020 (7.6% per year; 95% CI, 5.2% to 10.0% per year), followed by a decline (-7.0% per year; 95% CI, -11.8% to -1.9% per year).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study using Australian national administrative data, trends in violence against children differed substantially across systems. Although police data indicated increased violence exposure, particularly in recent years, child-protection substantiations and hospitalizations remained stable or declined. Strengthened national surveillance is critical.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Patient Navigation Plus mHealth Incentives for Linkage to OUD Care for Adults Who Also Use Methamphetamines: A Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Hospitalization is common among people with opioid use disorder (OUD) and is recognized as a reachable moment to start treatment. Methamphetamine use among people with OUD is associated with decreased linkage to postdischarge OUD care.

Objective: To determine the feasibility, acceptability, and exploratory clinical outcomes of a pilot randomized clinical trial (RCT) of an adherence-focused mobile health (mHealth) intervention aiming to increase linkage to and retention in outpatient buprenorphine services for patients hospitalized with OUD and methamphetamine use.

Design, setting, and participants: This single-site, 2-arm pilot RCT was conducted from January 3, 2024, to April 14, 2025, at a single-site, large urban safety net hospital in Seattle, Washington. Patients 18 years or older were eligible if they had initiated buprenorphine for OUD while in the hospital and had used methamphetamine within the past 30 days. Participants were randomized to the mHealth Incentivized Adherence Plus Patient Navigation (MIAPP) intervention or to treatment as usual (TAU).

Intervention: The MIAPP intervention combined financial incentives via mHealth-based adherence monitoring with a patient navigator (PN) during the first 30 days after discharge.

Main outcomes and measures: Feasibility was assessed by meeting the target enrollment of 40 participants and intervention delivery. Acceptability was measured by patient satisfaction ratings on a scale from 0 to 10, with 0 indicating not at all satisfied and 10 indicating extremely satisfied. The main pilot clinical outcome was linkage to outpatient OUD care within 30 days of hospital discharge, defined as medications for OUD being prescribed or dispensed. Other outcomes included retention in buprenorphine treatment and hospital readmissions at 90 days; past 30-day methamphetamine use was measured at the 30-day follow-up visit.

Results: The target enrollment of 40 participants (mean [SD] age, 43.4 [12.6] years) was met. Most participants (33 [82.5%]) were male. The intervention was allocated to 20 participants and delivered to 19 (95.0%); 20 participants received TAU. Participants reported being highly satisfied with the PN, with a mean (SD) patient satisfaction rating of 9.9 (0.3). Linkage to OUD care at 30 days occurred in 11 participants (55.0%) in the intervention arm compared with 10 (50.0%) in the TAU arm (risk ratio, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.61-1.99).

Conclusions and relevance: In this pilot RCT of the MIAPP intervention, study procedures were feasible and acceptable. While no difference in linkage rates was noted in this pilot study, larger studies are needed to determine intervention effectiveness.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Federal Immigration Enforcement Deployment and Emergency Department Utilization Among Children
item.description:
Importance: Heightened immigration enforcement in the US has been associated with reduced health care utilization in immigrant communities. Pediatric emergency departments (EDs) serve as a critical safety net for children, yet the impacts of acute immigration enforcement activity in pediatric ED utilization remain incompletely characterized.

Objective: To evaluate whether deployment of federal law enforcement in Washington, DC, was associated with changes in pediatric ED utilization and whether these changes differed by the patients' preferred language, race, and ethnicity.

Design, setting, and participants: This repeated cross-sectional interrupted time series analysis compared daily pediatric ED visits from June 1 to September 30, 2025, with visits in the same calendar period in 2024 at a single pediatric ED at a freestanding children's hospital in Washington, DC. Participants included all patients younger than 26 years presenting to the pediatric ED during the study period.

Exposures: Deployment of federal law enforcement personnel, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and National Guard troops, in Washington, DC, beginning August 11, 2025.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was daily pediatric ED visit counts. Interrupted time series models estimated immediate changes in ED utilization and postdeployment trends by patient-preferred language, race, and ethnicity, adjusting for age, sex, and acuity.

Results: A total of 21 822 pediatric ED visits were included in the analysis (median age, 6.5 [IQR, 2.0-13.1] years; 11 505 visits [52.7%] by male patients). Among these visits, 6253 patients (28.7%) identified as Hispanic, 10 649 (48.8%) as non-Hispanic Black, 2200 (10.1%) as non-Hispanic White, 558 (2.6%) as non-Hispanic multiracial, 1411 (6.5%) as non-Hispanic additional race, and 652 (3.0%), unknown. Patients who preferred to speak Spanish experienced an estimated immediate change in visits following federal deployment of -10.4 visits per day, whereas patients who preferred English experienced an estimated immediate change of 5.6 visits per day (difference, -16.0 visits per day). Hispanic patients similarly experienced an estimated immediate change of -13.3 visits per day, whereas non-Hispanic patients experienced an estimated immediate change of 6.2 visits per day (difference, -19.4 visits per day). Among Hispanic patients, those preferring Spanish had greater estimated immediate changes (-12.1 visits per day) than those preferring English (-0.8 visits per day; difference, -11.3 visits per day). No significant differences were observed across non-Hispanic racial and ethnic groups. No comparable declines were observed during the same period in 2024.

Conclusion and relevance: In this repeated cross-sectional study of pediatric ED visits before and after a federal immigration enforcement deployment, heightened immigration enforcement activity was associated with an immediate reduction in pediatric ED utilization, particularly among patients who preferred to speak Spanish. These findings suggest that immigration enforcement may have unintended consequences for children's use of emergency care.

item.description:
Importance: The 21st Century Cures Act made clinical notes broadly accessible to patients. However, the frequency and patient-perceived consequences of disrespectful or judgmental language (DJL) in medical records among the general US population remain unknown.

Objectives: To (1) quantify the frequency of participant-reported DJL in medical records; (2) characterize patient-anticipated consequences; and (3) examine factors associated with DJL and documentation trust in clinicians.

Design, setting, and participants: Cross-sectional, nationally weighted survey of 500 US adults conducted from November 21 to December 4, 2025, using YouGov's nonprobability-based online panel.

Main outcomes and measures: Descriptive statistics characterized experience of DJL in medical records (patient portal users) or health care (nonportal users) and patient-anticipated consequences. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% CIs were estimated using multivariable logistic regression including sociodemographics and clinical factors for 2 outcomes: DJL and documentation trust.

Results: Among 500 respondents (mean [SE] age, 48.0 [0.9] years; 253 [51.0%] women, 53 [11.0%] Black, 80 [18.0%] Hispanic [any race], and 315 [60.0%] White, 358 portal users [71.2%]), a total of 83 participants reported DJL: 58 of 358 (17.1%) portal users in their own medical records and/or that of a loved one, and 25 of 142 nonportal users (15.6%) in health care encounters. Patient-reported consequences included 377 of 500 respondents (74.7%) who anticipated DJL would influence subsequent care from a new clinician, and 373 (73.3%) who anticipated worse health outcomes, such as wrong medication prescribing or diagnostic errors. Furthermore, 435 of 500 respondents (85.5%) anticipated they would be less likely to return to the clinician. In adjusted analyses, patients who reported low income (compared with high income: aOR, 2.64; 95% CI, 1.18-5.91; P = .03) had a greater likelihood of reporting DJL, as did those with a diagnosis of chronic pain (compared with no diagnosis of chronic pain: aOR, 3.25; 95% CI, 1.46-7.26; P = .004). The experience of DJL was associated with diminished documentation trust in clinicians (aOR, 5.76; 95% CI, 2.90-11.46; P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this survey study, 1 in 6 US adults reported DJL in medical records (or in health care experiences for nonportal users), disproportionately affecting those with low income or chronic pain, and DJL was associated with diminished clinician documentation trust. Patient-anticipated consequences such as diminished intent to return to clinician suggest important quality of care and system-level implications. Realizing the promise of health information transparency will require concurrent reform in respectful language in clinical documentation and health care encounters.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Out-of-Pocket Costs for Chronic Illness Management in High-Deductible Health Plans
item.description:
Importance: High-deductible health plans (HDHPs) enroll a substantial share of privately insured Americans and are associated with reduced use of care, even care that is considered medically necessary. However, the magnitude of patient out-of-pocket (OOP) costs required to obtain evidence-based medical care when enrolled in HDHPs remains poorly understood.

Objective: To estimate patient OOP costs required to receive guideline-concordant care for common chronic conditions when enrolled in an HDHP vs a non-HDHP.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study used 2022 to 2023 national commercial insurance claims data. Participants included adults aged 18 to 64 years with employer-sponsored insurance and previously diagnosed diabetes, hypertension, or both. To enter the cohort, persons had to have received guideline-concordant care for their chronic illnesses. Data were analyzed from July 2025 to April 2026.

Exposure: Enrollment in an HDHP vs a non-HDHP.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was annual patient OOP costs to receive evidence-based care. Entropy balancing and generalized linear models with geographic fixed effects estimated the mean OOP costs of receiving minimum recommended medical care for diabetes, hypertension, or both in HDHPs and non-HDHPs. Estimates were weighted to ensure that observed costs were representative of the full sample of chronically ill persons.

Results: There were 539 590 adults receiving guideline-concordant care who entered the cohort. After entropy balancing, groups exhibited mean covariate balance, with males representing 57.9% of HDHP enrollees and 57.8% of non-HDHP enrollees, and similar age distributions across groups, with 45.4% of both HDHP and non-HDHP enrollees 55 to 64 years of age. item.description:
Importance: Recent trials have not demonstrated a benefit of endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) over medical therapy in acute stroke due to medium vessel occlusion (MeVO). However, it remains uncertain whether selected patients with favorable perfusion may benefit from EVT.

Objective: To investigate the association between perfusion mismatch profiles and functional outcomes in MeVO stroke and to determine whether these profiles modify the effect of EVT.

Design, setting, and participants: This study was a post hoc analysis of ESCAPE-MeVO (Endovascular Treatment to Improve Outcomes for Medium Vessel Occlusion), a multicenter randomized clinical trial conducted in North America, Europe, and the United Kingdom between April 2022 and June 2024, with a 90-day follow-up. Trial participants included patients with acute MeVO stroke presenting within 12 hours from last known well and evidence of salvageable brain tissue. This analysis included only patients with interpretable baseline perfusion imaging. Data were analyzed from March to July 2026.

Interventions: Randomization to EVT plus usual care vs usual care alone.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the 90-day ordinal modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score. Secondary outcomes included 24-hour follow-up infarct volume and 90-day mRS score of 0 to 1 and 0 to 2. Perfusion mismatch ratio and volume were defined as the ratio and difference between the critically hypoperfused area and the ischemic core, with volume thresholds defined by site-specific postprocessing software.

Results: Of 530 enrolled patients, 309 (58.3%) had available baseline perfusion imaging and were included in this study (EVT: n = 146; usual care: n = 163). Patient median (IQR) age was 73 (63-82) years, and 141 (45.6%) were women. Median (IQR) perfusion mismatch volume was 37.2 (22.1-57.2) mL, and the median (IQR) mismatch ratio was 6.1 (2.8-10.0). Ordinal 90-day mRS score was not associated with perfusion mismatch volume (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 1.03 [95% CI, 0.99-1.07] per 10-mL increase) or perfusion mismatch ratio (AOR, 1.03 [95% CI, 0.97-1.09] per 1-unit increase). There was no modification of EVT effect by perfusion mismatch volume or ratio on ordinal 90-day mRS. Results were consistent across secondary outcomes and subgroups.

Conclusions and relevance: In this exploratory post hoc analysis of acute MeVO stroke, perfusion mismatch profiles were not associated with functional outcomes and did not modify the effect of EVT. These findings suggest that perfusion imaging profiles based on currently used thresholds and cutoffs did not identify patients likely to benefit from EVT in the ESCAPE-MeVO trial.

Background: Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) are a major cause of morbidity after lung resection, particularly in older adults. item.title: Chest: Dominant lung involvement and heterozygous IFIH1 variants
item.description:
Background: Heterozygous gain-of-function (GoF) variants in IFIH1 are associated with rare autoinflammatory diseases characterized by heightened interferons-stimulated gene (ISG) signatures. These include Aicardi-Goutières syndrome, presenting with slowly progressive spastic paraparesis of the lower limbs, intracerebral calcifications, and neuroinflammation, and Singleton-Merten syndrome, defined by tooth loss, bone demineralization, and vascular calcification.

Research question: Do rare IFIH1 GoF variants contribute to an interstitial lung disease phenotype, thereby expanding the spectrum of IFIH1-related disorders?

Study design and methods: Among 559 children with interstitial lung disease (chILD) and exome sequencing as part of their diagnostic work-up, 12 rare heterozygous IFIH1 variants were identified. Of these, 10 were missense variants of unknown significance, which were functionally assessed in vitro using luciferase assay and ISG-expression profiling. Genome-wide RNA analysis was performed on available patient samples to explore broader transcriptional effects.

Results: Four variants with increased basal IFNβ transcription in vitro and elevated ISG expression in vivo indicating GoF behaviour were identified. Disease severity correlated with GoF potential of the respective variant. Two patients harbouring IFIH1 variants with strong GoF activity displayed multisystem involvement and died from respiratory failure at 3 and 4 months of age, respectively. Two additional patients showed milder phenotypes with chronic lung disease stabilizing by the age of 8 and 10 years, respectively. Lung biopsies showed alveolar hypoplasia and alveolar macrophage pneumonia (=desquamative interstitial pneumonia) of varying severity.

Interpretation: We report a dominant interstitial lung disease phenotype in individuals harbouring novel IFIH1 variants, expanding IFIH1-related disease to the group of type I interferonopathies with pulmonary manifestations like STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy (SAVI) and COPA syndrome.

item.title: Resuscitation: Mechanical versus manual bag-valve ventilation during cardiopulmonary resuscitation in adults with cardiac arrest: A systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis
item.description:
Background/objective: Optimal ventilation delivery during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) remains uncertain. Current resuscitation guidelines do not recommend mechanical ventilation (MV) over manual bag-valve ventilation (BV). We evaluated the association between MV use during CPR and clinical outcomes in adults with cardiac arrest compared with manual BV.

Methods: We searched 6 bibliographic databases from inception through May 31, 2026. Included studies compared MV and BV ventilation CPR in adult cardiac arrest patients. Patients receiving MV at any moment during CPR were classified as the MV group; those receiving only BV comprised the BV group. Primary outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to hospital admission, survival to hospital discharge, and good neurological outcome. Secondary outcomes included physiologic variables and pneumothorax. We calculated pooled risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences with 95% credible intervals (CrIs) using Bayesian random-effects meta-analyses.

Results: Eight studies involving 6,847 patients were included. For the primary outcome, MV use during CPR was associated with a higher rate of ROSC than BV use (pooled RR, 1.20; 95% CrI, 1.04 to 1.42), with a 99% posterior probability of benefit. Posterior probabilities favoring MV for survival to admission, survival to discharge, and favorable neurological outcome were 92.3%, 93.6%, and 92.2%, respectively. Pneumothorax incidence was similar between groups.

Conclusion: In adult cardiac arrest, MV use during CPR was associated with higher ROSC compared with manual BV. Evidence for improved survival and neurological outcomes remains imprecise and inconclusive.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Delayed diagnosis of a traumatic gluteal pseudoaneurysm with arteriovenous fistula and dual arterial supply mimicking a buttock abscess after a stab wound: a case report
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Traumatic arteriovenous fistulas (AVFs), with or without associated pseudoaneurysms, are uncommon complications of penetrating vascular injuries that may cause substantial morbidity and potentially fatal complications. Evidence is largely derived from case reports and case series, with important contributions from military experience. Delayed gluteal lesions may mimic a hematoma or abscess, creating a diagnostic pitfall.

Case presentation: A 51-year-old male presented with a one-month history of a progressively enlarging painful left buttock mass following a stab wound that had been primarily sutured at a local hospital. Initial ultrasound suggested a hematoma, and the patient was admitted with a working diagnosis of "left buttock mass." Physical examination revealed a 7 × 7 cm fluctuant mass with tenderness but without overt signs of infection. Contrast-enhanced pelvic CT demonstrated a 6.8 × 3.2 cm intensely enhancing lesion within the left gluteus maximus with prominent feeding vessels, suggestive of an arteriovenous fistula or vascular malformation. Digital subtraction angiography confirmed a left gluteal pseudoaneurysm with an associated arteriovenous fistula supplied by branches of both the inferior gluteal and internal pudendal arteries, with early venous opacification. The patient underwent successful transcatheter embolization using fibered platinum coils and a cyanoacrylate-lipiodol mixture, with complete occlusion of the fistula confirmed on completion angiography. The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day 2. At three-month follow-up, the patient reported no specific discomfort, and color Doppler ultrasonography showed a marked reduction in mass size with no detectable flow within the lesion.

Conclusion: Penetrating buttock trauma may cause a gluteal pseudoaneurysm with an associated AVF supplied by more than one internal iliac artery branch. Contrast-enhanced CT and selective angiography are important for recognizing the vascular lesion and delineating all feeding arteries. In this patient, embolization of both the inferior gluteal and internal pudendal arterial feeders achieved complete angiographic occlusion and a favorable clinical outcome, with a markedly smaller mass and no detectable intralesional flow on color Doppler ultrasonography at three months.
