item.title: Ann Intern Med: Benzodiazepine Use Early in Pregnancy and Risk for Congenital Malformations
item.description:
Background: Existing data on malformations associated with benzodiazepine use in pregnancy are conflicting.

Objective: To assess the risk for major congenital malformations from first-trimester exposure to benzodiazepines.

Design: Population-based U.S. cohort study.

Setting: Medicaid (2000-2018) and Merative MarketScan (2003-2020) databases.

Participants: Pregnant persons enrolled from 90 days before pregnancy to 30 days after delivery, and their live-born infants enrolled for 90 days after birth.

Measurements: Exposure was defined as at least 1 fill of a benzodiazepine in the first trimester. Primary outcomes were any major congenital malformation and organ-specific malformations previously associated with benzodiazepine exposure. The investigators estimated relative risks (RRs) comparing exposed versus unexposed pregnancies with propensity score fine stratification weights to control for confounders. An RR of 1.3 or higher was prespecified as clinically significant.

Results: In total, 51 339 of 2 478 434 (2.1%) publicly insured and 27 779 of 1 750 721 (1.6%) commercially insured pregnancies had benzodiazepine exposure. The adjusted absolute risks for any malformation in exposed versus unexposed pregnancies were 4.0% versus 4.1% for Medicaid and 4.9% versus 4.8% for MarketScan. The pooled adjusted RR was 0.99 (95% CI, 0.96 to 1.03). Associations with organ-specific malformations were not consistently observed in sensitivity analyses, nor was a dose-response relationship observed. Analyses of different benzodiazepines yielded similar results. The risk for selected organ-specific malformations was increased in some analyses of coexposure to benzodiazepines and other psychoactive medications, but a consistent pattern did not emerge.

Limitations: Potential nondifferential exposure and outcome misclassification; analyses restricted to malformations prevalent at birth.

Conclusion: No substantial increase in the risk for malformations was consistently identified across data sources. Findings from coexposure analyses were inconsistent and warrant further study.

item.title: Ann Intern Med: How Would You Screen This 26-Year-Old Woman for Cervical Cancer? Grand Rounds Discussion From Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center
item.description:
Cervical cancer is the third most common gynecologic cancer, with more than 13 000 new cases diagnosed in 2025. The incidence of and mortality from cervical cancer vary across racial and ethnic groups and in persons living in medically underserved or geographically isolated areas, with half of all cervical cancers occurring in women who are underscreened or have never been screened. Persistent infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most important risk factor for cervical cancer and is associated with nearly all cases. Although genital tract HPV infection is common, most HPV infections are transient, and cervical cancer occurs in only a small portion of patients with HPV. For decades, cervical cancer screening relied on annual cytologic assessment. A growing understanding of the role of HPV infection in the natural progression of cervical cancer has led to updated screening recommendations from the American Cancer Society and the Women's Preventive Services Initiative, as well as a draft update from the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. These recommendations include primary HPV testing as a preferred screening strategy and include an option for self-collected specimens for HPV testing. Here, 2 experts in this field, a primary care physician and an obstetrics and gynecology physician, debate how to apply these guidelines when screening a patient for cervical cancer. They discuss a range of screening options and consider the challenges of applying these guidelines across different age groups and in patients at increased risk.

item.description:
Delirium is a common, acute confusional state that is associated with adverse patient, caregiver, and health system outcomes. All patients are at risk for delirium, although those with advanced age or acute infection and those taking sedatives and anticholinergics are at greater risk. The pathophysiology of delirium is complex and includes neuronal injury, inflammation, metabolic imbalance, and blood-brain barrier disruption. It is important to note that delirium is preventable; recognizing people at risk and identifying and addressing predisposing and precipitating factors is paramount. item.title: JAMA: Development and Validation of an Adult Medical Urgency Score for US Donor Heart Allocation
item.description:
Importance: One in 5 heart transplant candidates in the US die or are delisted without transplant. Donor hearts are currently allocated by a 6-status therapy-based system criticized for limited risk stratification and susceptibility to gaming.

Objective: To develop a new heart allocation policy based on an objective medical urgency score that ranks candidates based on the interaction between physiology and mechanical circulatory support.

Design, setting, and participants: Registry-based observational study using data from the US organ transplant system. All adult (aged ≥18 years) heart transplant candidates from January 2019 to August 2025 were included, split into training (2019-2023), validation (2023-2024), and test (2024-2025) datasets.

Main outcomes and measures: A marginal structural model of 6-week mortality without transplant was estimated (the US Candidate Risk Score [US-CRS]). Eight models were compared in held-out data by weighted time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and calibration by status. Finally, US-CRS was converted into an allocation policy and a match-run simulation of waitlist reordering was performed compared with the current 6-status system.

Results: Adult heart transplant candidates were partitioned into consecutive training (n = 21 859), validation (n = 7897), and test (n = 8256) datasets (mean [SD] age, 53 [13] years; 74% male). The chosen US-CRS model included 5 laboratory values and 4 therapeutic devices (durable left ventricular assist device, intra-aortic balloon pump, microaxial flow pump, and advanced mechanical circulatory support). In test-set cross-sections of candidates actively waiting on the same calendar date, US-CRS had similar or significantly higher time-dependent AUC than the current 6-status system (mean AUC, 0.807 vs 0.693, respectively) and acceptable calibration by status, especially for candidates who received their status by exception. In match-run analysis (n = 45 530 donor hearts), a US-CRS-based system led to 67% of transplant recipients moving down in rank order and increased observed 6-week transplant-censored mortality for the first candidate on the match run from 11.2% (95% CI, 10.1%-12.5%) under the current system to 15.7% (95% CI, 13.9%-17.6%) under the US-CRS-based system.

Conclusions and relevance: In this registry-based study of US heart transplant candidates, a US-CRS-based allocation system prioritized sicker candidates with higher mortality without transplant compared with the current medical urgency statuses.

item.title: JAMA Intern Med: Communicating Uncertainties About the Benefits and Risks of New Cancer Drugs: Two Randomized Clinical Trials
item.description:
Importance: Cancer drugs are frequently approved based on uncertain benefits and risks that are not communicated to patients.

Objective: To evaluate the effect of communicating uncertainties about the benefits and risks of new cancer drugs on changes in individuals' hypothetical decisions to take the drug.

Design, setting, and participants: Two randomized clinical trials recruited online a demographically diverse sample of US adults (census matched for age, sex, education, income, and race and ethnicity) from May 9 to July 26, 2025.

Intervention: Plain-language statements describing uncertainties about drug benefits and risks. Trial 1 randomized participants to 1 of 5 uncertainties: (1) single-arm trial design, (2) unrepresentative population in terms of race and ethnicity, (3) short study duration, (4) surrogate end point, or (5) no noticeable improvement. Trial 2 randomized participants to 1, 2, 3, or 4 uncertainties or to a control group.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome in trial 1 was changes in hypothetical decisions to take a new cancer drug (within-group difference), while in trial 2 the primary outcome was the change in between-group differences in hypothetical decisions (control vs intervention groups). Secondary outcomes included perceived treatment effectiveness, worry associated with taking the drug, and trust in the information and the US Food and Drug Administration.

Results: A total of 6272 adults were included in the primary analysis (3102 [49.5%] women). In trial 1, learning about uncertainties reduced hypothetical decisions to take the drug by a mean of 10.1 percentage points (pp; 95% CI, -11.7 to -8.5 pp; P < .001). The reduction in hypothetical decisions to take the drug was observed for all uncertainties, including among those in the group that learned that it was unknown whether patients would notice an improvement with the drug (-14.1 pp; 95% CI, -17.9 to -10.4 pp; P < .001) and those who learned that the drug was not studied in patients of similar race or ethnicity (-12.8 pp; 95% CI, -16.4 to -9.2; P < .001). In trial 2, hypothetical decisions to take the drug decreased with each additional uncertainty, demonstrating a dose-dependent effect. Learning about uncertainties reduced perceived effectiveness and trust but did not affect worry.

Conclusions and relevance: In 2 randomized clinical trials including a demographically diverse sample of US adults, learning about common uncertainties with a new cancer drug's benefits and risks reduced hypothetical decisions to take the drug.

Secondary outcomes assessed treatment escalation, complications of severe alcohol withdrawal syndrome, and resource utilization. Targeted maximum likelihood estimation with ensemble machine learning was used to estimate marginal mean differences and risk differences between exposure groups.

item.description:
Importance: Heart failure affects more than 6 million US adults; approximately 4% to 5% progress to advanced disease despite optimal therapy. Heart transplant is a class I guideline-recommended therapy for select individuals with advanced heart failure.

Observations: Early referral for heart transplant is guided by the "I NEED HELP" mnemonic, a tool that identifies patients with advanced heart failure based on criteria such as use of inotropes, persistent symptoms (New York Heart Association class III or IV), end-organ dysfunction, left ventricular ejection fraction, defibrillator shocks, hospitalizations for heart failure, persistent edema or escalating use of diuretics, and low blood pressure. Each criterion is associated with higher risk of death or first heart failure hospitalization over a median follow-up of 260 days (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.19 [95% CI, 1.11-1.27] for each additional criterion). Typical absolute contraindications to heart transplant include active systemic infection, malignancy with limited life expectancy, severe and irreversible end-organ dysfunction (eg, cirrhosis, severe pulmonary hypertension), active substance use, major untreated psychiatric illness, inadequate social support, and severe frailty. Approximately 4600 heart transplants are performed annually in the US. The mortality rate was 8.5 deaths/100 patient-years for adults on the transplant waiting list in 2023. Leading causes of early death after transplant include primary graft dysfunction (39.5%), multiorgan failure (18.5%), and infection (13.9%). Among adults, contemporary survival rates after heart transplant are 91.5% at 1 year and 80.3% at 5 years. Lifelong maintenance immunosuppression typically combines a calcineurin inhibitor, antiproliferative agents (typically mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine) and corticosteroids, with selective use of induction therapy (intensive immunosuppression immediately after transplant). Acute rejection requiring treatment occurs in 20% to 25% of recipients within a year, and may be treated with high-dose corticosteroids, antithymocyte globulin, and B-cell-targeted therapies (such as rituximab or bortezomib). Rejection surveillance with endomyocardial biopsies of the right ventricular septum is performed 5 to 10 times within the first year after transplant. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (chronic rejection that causes diffuse coronary narrowing) affects 29% of heart transplant recipients within 5 years and 46.8% by 10 years and is the leading cause of late mortality. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy is treated with statins, mechanistic target of rapamycin inhibitors (such as sirolimus or everolimus), and retransplant for severe cases. Infections (62.5% are bacterial, 30.0% are viral, 6.7% are fungal, and 0.8% are parasitic) and malignancy (10.7% within 5 years after heart transplant) are other leading causes of late mortality.

Conclusions and relevance: Heart transplant is the definitive therapy for carefully selected patients with advanced heart failure despite receiving optimal, guideline-directed therapy. After heart transplant, lifelong multidisciplinary care is necessary to manage immunosuppression, prevent and treat rejection and cardiac allograft vasculopathy, and monitor for infection and malignancy.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Home-Based Programs and Cardiac Rehabilitation Participation Among Veterans With Ischemic Heart Disease
item.description:
Importance: Cardiac rehabilitation (CR) is a guideline-recommended secondary prevention program that reduces morbidity and mortality among patients with ischemic heart disease (IHD) yet remains underutilized. Over the past decade, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) has implemented strategies to increase CR participation, including expansion of virtual home-based CR (HBCR) programs as alternatives to traditional center-based CR (CBCR).

Objective: To examine temporal trends and factors associated with CR participation among veterans with IHD.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study used national VHA electronic health record data to evaluate CR participation among veterans hospitalized for IHD, identified using International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision (ICD-9), ICD-10, or Current Procedural Terminology codes from 2012 to 2022. Data were analyzed from October 25, 2025, to July 25, 2026.

Exposures: Availability of CR delivery models at Veterans Affairs (VA) facilities, including referral to community care programs only, VA CBCR, or VA HBCR.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the proportion of eligible veterans with acute myocardial infarction, percutaneous coronary intervention, or coronary artery bypass graft surgery who participated in any type of CR within 12 months of the index event, identified using Current Procedural Terminology codes and VA stop codes from VA-provided, VA-purchased, or Medicare-claimed services. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with CR participation.

Results: Among 405 907 veterans with IHD (mean [SD] age, 68.5 [11.1] years; 391 998 men [96.6%]), 63 185 (15.6%) participated in CR. Participation increased from 9.6% in 2012 to 17.1% in 2022, with a peak of 19.7% in 2018. In 2022, participation was higher at facilities offering HBCR (20.0%) compared with those offering CBCR without HBCR (14.8%) or referral to community care programs only (14.3%). The adjusted odds ratio (AOR) of participation among veterans treated at facilities offering HBCR was 1.80 (95% CI, 1.75-1.84), whereas the AOR of participation at facilities offering CBCR without HBCR was 1.29 (95% CI, 1.26-1.32) compared with referral to community care programs only.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of veterans with IHD, participation in CR nearly doubled between 2012 and 2022. Patients who had index events at facilities offering HBCR had higher CR participation than those at facilities offering CBCR without HBCR, or at facilities offering only referral to community care. Broader availability of HBCR programs may help improve participation within large health systems.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Maternal Prenatal Diet and Colic and Eczema Among Infants
item.description:
Importance: Infantile colic is a disorder of gut-brain interaction whose cause is poorly understood.

Objective: To estimate associations of maternal diet quality and intakes of specific allergenic foods with infant eczema and colic.

Design, setting, and participants: Project Viva prospective cohort of 2128 mother-child pairs unselected for atopic risk with recruitment in early pregnancy in Eastern Massachusetts from April 1999 to November 2002, with follow-up to October 2003, and data analysis November 2025 to July 2026.

Exposures: Prenatal diet via food frequency questionnaires in early pregnancy (median [IQR], 9.9 [8.8-11.3] weeks) and midpregnancy (median [IQR], 27.9 [26.7-28.8] weeks). The Mediterranean Diet Score (MDS) and Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII) were calculated and intake of commonly allergenic foods was determined.

Main outcomes and measures: Maternal report of colic symptoms and eczema diagnosis at median (IQR) of 6.3 (6.0-6.8) months.

Results: Among 1324 pairs with exposure and outcome data, mean (SD) maternal age was 32.6 (4.6) years, 667 (50.4%) were nulliparous, and 532 (40.2%) reported a history of atopy; 152 (11.5%) infants had eczema alone, 273 (20.6%) had colic alone, and 61 (4.6%) had both. In multinomial logistic regression models adjusted for maternal age, race, ethnicity, education, parity, smoking, and atopy, greater mean (SD) MDS (4.6 [2.0] points) was associated with lower odds of colic and eczema (odds ratio [OR], 0.85; 95% CI, 0.74-0.98 per 1 point), and mean (SD) DII (-2.7 [1.3]) was associated with higher odds (OR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.12-1.61 per 1 point). Neither diet score was associated with eczema or colic alone. Seafood intake was associated with lower odds of colic and eczema combined (OR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.58-0.97 per weekly serving). Nut intake was associated with higher risk for colic among those without eczema (eg, OR, 1.05; 95% CI, 1.00-1.09 per weekly serving of any nuts or peanuts), but not with colic and eczema combined (OR, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.88-1.07). Dairy or egg intakes were not associated with any outcomes. Associations of dietary scores and fish intake with colic were stronger among infants of atopic mothers.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of 1324 mother-child pairs, poorer maternal diet quality and lower seafood intake were associated with infantile colic with eczema or maternal atopic history.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Immunohistochemistry vs Molecular Breast Cancer Subtyping Among African Populations
item.description:
Importance: Breast cancer subtyping based on immunohistochemistry (IHC) guides systemic therapy where gene expression profiling assays are unavailable, yet its validity against molecular reference standards remains poorly characterized in African populations, where laboratory infrastructure and access to pathology services are limited.

Objective: To evaluate concordance between IHC-based breast cancer subtyping and PAM50 intrinsic subtypes in East and West African populations and identify resource-appropriate strategies to improve classification.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study included Kenyan (diagnosed 2012-2022) and Ghanaian women (diagnosed 2013-2015) with invasive breast cancer, from whom formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor specimens were collected during the same periods. Gene expression profiling and data analyses were performed between April 2020 and August 2026 for both cohorts.

Exposures: Tumor subtyping using standard IHC markers (estrogen receptor [ER], progesterone receptor [PR], and ERBB2 status and Ki-67) and histologic grade vs PAM50 intrinsic subtyping derived from a gene expression panel.

Main outcomes and measures: Concordance between IHC-based and PAM50 intrinsic subtypes was assessed using Cohen κ statistics, with sensitivity and specificity calculated against PAM50.

Results: Among 460 women in Kenya with breast cancer (mean [SD] age at diagnosis, 50.3 [12.5] years), 224 (49.4%) had grade 3 disease and 148 (42.3%) had stage III or IV tumors. A total of 451 women in Ghana with breast cancer (mean [SD] age, 49.9 [12.0] years; 317 [75.1%] with grade 3 disease) were enrolled as a validation cohort. PAM50 classified patients' tumors as luminal A (201 tumors [43.7%]), luminal B (82 tumors [17.8%]), ERBB2-enriched (50 tumors [10.9%]), basal-like (99 tumors [21.5%]), and normal-like (28 tumors [6.1%]). Concordance between IHC and PAM50 was highest for basal-like tumors (sensitivity ranging from 73.3% [95% CI, 61.9%-82.9%] to 79.6% [95% CI, 70.3%-87.1%]; specificity ranging from 96.9% [95% CI, 93.9%-98.6%] to 97.3% [95% CI, 94.9%-98.7%]) and moderate for ERBB2-enriched tumors (sensitivity was 50.0% across all schemes, with 95% CIs ranging from 33.8%-66.2% to 35.5%-64.5%; specificity ranging from 97.6% [95% CI, 95.6%-98.9%] to 97.9% [95% CI, 95.6%-99.2%]). Luminal subtypes showed substantial misclassification using ER, PR, and ERBB2 status alone. Incorporation of Ki-67 (≥20%) or histologic grade improved discrimination between luminal A and luminal B tumors, increasing luminal B classification from 12.2% (95% CI, 8.5%-16.7%) to 41.2% (95% CI, 35.2%-47.4%), even when PR status was excluded from the panel. Findings were independently validated in women with breast cancer from Ghana.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of African breast cancer populations, standard IHC markers performed well for basal-like tumors but frequently misclassified luminal subtypes without proliferation markers. When testing was constrained, proliferation markers contributed more to molecular approximation than PR, with histologic grade providing useful information when Ki-67 was unavailable. These findings support tiered, resource-adapted classification where molecular assays are inaccessible.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Influenza Vaccination Preferences Among Adults Aged 60 Years and Older in Beijing, China
item.description:
Importance: Influenza vaccination coverage among older adults remains suboptimal in China despite free vaccination policies in some regions. Understanding their preferences may inform strategies to improve uptake.

Objective: To quantify preferences for influenza vaccination attributes and assess preference heterogeneity by prior influenza vaccination history.

Design, setting, and participants: This community-based survey study was conducted at 2 districts in Beijing, China, where influenza vaccination is provided free of charge for adults aged 60 years or older. A convenience sample of adults aged 60 years or older was included from 6 Beijing subdistricts and participated in a discrete choice experiment conducted from August to September 2025.

Main outcomes and measures: Stated choice among 2 hypothetical influenza vaccination profiles and an opt-out option. Attributes included vaccine effectiveness, risk of mild adverse effects, vaccination venue and operating hours, outreach method, information source, and message content. Conditional logit, mixed logit, scenario simulations, and vaccination-history interaction analyses were performed.

Results: Among 514 participants included in the analyses, the median age was 71 years (IQR, 65-79 years), and 356 (69.3%) were women. Higher vaccine effectiveness was associated with greater vaccination preference (β = 2.12; 95% CI, 1.37 to 2.88), whereas higher perceived risk of mild adverse effects was associated with lower preference (β = -5.53; 95% CI, -7.83 to -3.22). Participants preferred community-based vaccination settings, telephone reminders (β = 1.06; 95% CI, 0.76 to 1.36), information from government or community organizations (β = 0.78; 95% CI, 0.54 to 1.02), and messages emphasizing protection of family members (β = 0.50; 95% CI, 0.26 to 0.74). Increasing vaccine effectiveness from 20% to 80% and reducing perceived risk of adverse effects from 20% to 5% were associated with 30.74- and 19.96-percentage-point (pp) increases in the model-estimated choice probability, respectively. Compared with participants with prior vaccination, never-vaccinated participants had a greater preference for opting out (difference in β = 1.07; 95% CI, 0.11 to 2.03), greater sensitivity to mild adverse effect risk (difference in β per 10-pp increase, -0.49; 95% CI, -0.93 to -0.05), and lower responsiveness to vaccine effectiveness (difference in β per 10-pp increase, -0.18; 95% CI, -0.31 to -0.04).

Conclusions and relevance: In this discrete choice experiment of older adults in Beijing, influenza vaccination preferences were associated with vaccine profiles, trusted communication, and community-based service delivery. Prior vaccination history identified differences in benefit-risk weighting that may inform broad and targeted vaccination strategies.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Depression and Anxiety Risk in Children With Intellectual Developmental Disorder
item.description:
Importance: Population-based pediatric data on depression and anxiety incidence among children with intellectual developmental disorder (IDD), particularly in Asian populations, are limited.

Objective: To investigate associations between IDD and depression and anxiety incidence and evaluate moderating factors.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study used linked data from South Korea's National Health Insurance Service database and National Disability Registry from 2004 to 2020. Children aged 2 to 17 years with newly registered IDD were matched 1:3 by sex and birth year to children without developmental disorders. Follow-up continued until 2023. Data were analyzed from April 20 to July 9, 2025.

Exposure: Intellectual developmental disorder among children and adolescents.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was incident depression and anxiety as defined by International Statistical Classification of Disease, Tenth Revision codes. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs for developing depression or anxiety were estimated using multivariable-adjusted Cox proportional hazards regression models.

Results: Among 236 132 children (mean [SD] age, 9.3 [4.3] years; 64.2% male), 59 033 (25.0%) had IDD. Among children with IDD, 20.1% were diagnosed with depression and 21.9% with anxiety at least 1 year after baseline. Compared with children without developmental disorders, children with IDD had higher risk of depression (HR, 2.18 [95% CI, 2.13-2.24]) and anxiety (HR, 1.85 [95% CI, 1.80-1.89]) after adjusting for sex, age, income level, residential location, and comorbidity burden. Compared with children without developmental disorders, risks of depression and anxiety, respectively, were higher among male children (adjusted HR [AHR], 2.46 [95% CI, 2.39-2.54] and 2.06 [95% CI, 2.00-2.12]), younger children (aged 2-5 years: AHR, 2.83 [95% CI, 2.66-3.01] and 2.41 [95% CI, 2.27-2.55]; aged 6-8 years: AHR, 2.51 [95% CI, 2.40-2.64] and 2.12 [95% CI, 2.02-2.22]), urban residents (AHR, 2.36 [95% CI, 2.25-2.48] and 1.97 [95% CI, 1.88-2.06]), and children with a mild comorbidity burden (Charlson Comorbidity Index score of 1) (AHR, 2.32 [95% CI, 2.22-2.43] and 1.98 [95% CI, 1.90-2.07]). Stratification by sex, younger age, and mild comorbidity burden consistently showed higher risks of depression and anxiety across both sexes with IDD compared with children without developmental disorders (all P < .001 for interaction). In males with IDD, rural residence was associated with higher depression risk (AHR, 2.71 [95% CI, 2.56-2.86]) and urban residence with higher anxiety risk (AHR, 2.15 [95% CI, 2.04-2.28]). In females with IDD, depression and anxiety, respectively, were associated with lower income (AHR, 2.08 [95% CI, 1.86-2.34] and 1.76 [95% CI, 1.59-1.96]) and urban residence (AHR, 2.03 [95% CI, 1.88-2.20] and 1.73 [95% CI, 1.62-1.86]). Mild comorbidity burden was associated with increased risks of depression (AHR, 1.18 [95% CI, 1.07-1.31]) and anxiety (AHR, 1.16 [95% CI, 1.06-1.27]) for both sexes. Within the IDD cohort, female sex, older age, and lower income status were associated with higher risks of both outcomes (all P < .001 for trend).

Conclusions and relevance: This nationwide cohort study of more than 236 000 children and adolescents found that individuals with IDD, particularly males, younger children, and those with mild comorbidity burden, had increased depression and anxiety risks compared with individuals without developmental disorders. These findings underscore the need for targeted screening and interventions tailored to sociodemographic and comorbidity profiles.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Facility Access and Clinical Outcomes Among Patients With Acute Myocardial Infarction
item.description:
Importance: The proliferation of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) facilities across the US has raised questions about whether expanding capacity improves outcomes in areas already served vs those without prior access.

Objective: To evaluate the association between the opening of PCI-capable facilities and outcomes following acute myocardial infarction (AMI) in communities with and without baseline PCI access.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study used California data from inpatient, emergency department, and ambulatory surgery encounters from January 1, 2011, to December 31, 2022, including all adults hospitalized with a primary diagnosis of AMI. Zip code communities were categorized by baseline (2011) access to PCI-capable facilities within a 30-minute drive.

Exposure: Opening of a PCI-capable facility within 30 minutes of a community's zip code during the study period.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were (1) admission to a PCI-capable facility, (2) receipt of PCI during the index hospitalization, (3) unscheduled acute care visit within 30 days, and (4) all-cause mortality at 30 days and 1 year. Linear probability models with community and time-fixed effects estimated changes in outcomes following PCI facility openings separately for communities with and without baseline access.

Results: Among 590 282 patients with AMI (157 435 younger than age 60 years [27%]; 222 773 female [38%]; 63 460 Asian [11%], 129 137 Hispanic [22%], 315 326 White [53%]), 500 778 (85%) lived in communities with baseline PCI access, and 89 504 (15%) lived in communities without; 18 805 patients (21%) without baseline access experienced a PCI opening. Openings in communities without baseline access were associated with a 30.0 percentage point (pp) increase (95% CI, 28.2 to 31.8 pp) in admission to PCI-capable hospitals and a 5.1 pp increase (95% CI, 3.3 to 7.0 pp) in PCI receipt, along with reductions in 30-day (-1.8 pp; 95% CI, -3.2 to -0.5 pp) and 1-year (-2.8 pp; 95% CI, -4.7 to -1.0 pp) mortality. In contrast, openings in communities with baseline access were associated with smaller gains in admission (1.5 pp; 95% CI, 1.1 to 1.9 pp), modest increases in PCI use (1.0 pp; 95% CI, 0.5 to 1.6 pp), decreases in unscheduled visits within 30 days (-0.7 pp; 95% CI, -1.2 to -0.2 pp), and no mortality change. Sensitivity analyses restricted to higher-volume PCI centers (50 annual cases or more) yielded consistent findings.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of 590 282 patients with AMI in California, opening new PCI facilities was associated with substantial improvements in communities without prior PCI availability, including a 53% relative increase in access to admission, 16% increase in PCI use, and 20% and 15% reductions in 30-day and 1-year mortality, respectively. In contrast, already served areas showed smaller benefits and no mortality improvement. PCI expansion should prioritize underserved regions to maximize population-level benefits and avoid inefficient duplication of services.

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: Factors Associated with Low-Acuity EMS Transport to the Emergency Department: An Observational Study Guided by the Andersen Behavioral Model
item.description:
Objectives: Emergency medical services (EMS) demand is increasing, with a growing proportion of low-acuity encounters. Prior studies are limited by regional sampling, inconsistent definitions, narrow observation periods, and limited theoretical grounding. The objective of this study was to identify predisposing, enabling, and need-based factors associated with EMS transport among low-acuity emergency department (ED) patients, guided by Andersen's Behavioral Model of Health Services Use.

Methods: We conducted a secondary, retrospective observational study using a 10% random sample of multicenter electronic health record data from 21 EDs in the southeastern United States. Eligible visits included: 1) patient age >17 years, 2) occurred between January 1, 2016, and April 29, 2025, 3) triaged as Emergency Severity Index 4 or 5, and 4) ended in a final visit disposition of discharge. The primary outcome was arrival at the ED by EMS. We categorized independent variables as predisposing, enabling, or need-based factors according to Andersen's model. We used multivariable logistic regression to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Results: Among 41,761 low-acuity ED encounters, 3,232 (7.7%) arrived by EMS. Higher odds of EMS use were observed for older age (per 10-year increase; aOR 1.33, 95% CI = 1.30-1.36), male sex (aOR 1.20, 95% CI = 1.12-1.30), being retired or disabled (aOR 3.60, 95% CI = 3.15-4.10), being unemployed (aOR 2.26, 95% CI = 2.04-2.52), having a nighttime presentation (aOR 1.63, 95% CI = 1.51-1.76), and mental health diagnosis (aOR 1.76, 95% CI = 1.62-1.90). Lower odds of EMS arrival were observed for white race (aOR 0.89, 95% CI = 0.83-0.96), established primary care (aOR 0.57, 95% CI = 0.53-0.62), weekend presentation (aOR 0.91; 95% CI = 0.84-0.99), and visits during (aOR 0.63, 95% CI = 0.55-0.71) or after (aOR 0.54, 95% CI = 0.48-0.61) the COVID-19 period. Rurality, insurance, and primary language were not associated with EMS use.

Conclusions: Among low-acuity ED patients, EMS arrival was associated with older age, unemployment or disability, no established primary care clinician, and a previous mental health diagnosis. These characteristics identify a population that may be served by alternatives to ambulance transport, such as treat-in-place and alternative destination pathways, when paired with expanded access to primary care and behavioral health resources.

Objective: Emergency department (ED) human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) screening programs are designed primarily to identify persons with undiagnosed HIV and, therefore, systematically exclude persons with diagnosed HIV (PWHDx). PWHDx who are out of care (OOC) contribute disproportionately to HIV transmission and are a priority population within Ending the HIV Epidemic (EHE) initiatives. Because PWHDx OOC are not routinely identified through screening, complementary strategies are needed to support re-engagement in care. We evaluated an electronic health record algorithm (EHRa) designed to identify PWHDx presenting to the ED. We then determined HIV care status, characterized differences between patients in care (IC) and OOC, and quantified the incremental yield of EHRa-based identification beyond routine HIV screening.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional study across 3 EDs with universal HIV screening. Adults (≥18 years) presenting between February and July 2024 who screened HIV positive or were identified through the EHRa were included. Conclusions: A simple, locally generated EHRa substantially increased identification of PWHDx in the ED, including many OOC patients who were not captured through routine screening. A simple, locally generated EHRa demonstrated substantial incremental yield for identifying PWHDx in the ED, including many OOC patients who were not captured through routine screening. Objectives: Medetomidine, a veterinary alpha-2-adrenergic agonist, has emerged as a dominant adulterant in the Philadelphia illicit opioid supply, producing a severe withdrawal syndrome requiring significant inpatient support. We developed an intravenous dexmedetomidine protocol for intermediate care units (IMCU) and describe the safety and feasibility of delivering this care outside the intensive care unit (ICU).

Methods: A retrospective descriptive analysis of patients who received dexmedetomidine under an IMCU orderset for alpha-2 withdrawal was conducted at two urban medical centers in Philadelphia, PA, from April 2024 to February 2026. Encounters were classified as protocol-concordant or protocol-discordant by dosing and level of support; the concordant cohort was primary. Variables included demographics and addiction consult status. Outcomes included length of stay (hospital and IMCU), ICU admission, rapid response team activation, intubation, and discharge disposition.

Results: Of 487 encounters, 449 (92.2%) were protocol-concordant and 38 (7.8%) protocol-discordant. All subsequent results describe the protocol-concordant cohort (n=449) unless otherwise noted. The cohort was predominantly male (58.1%) with a mean age of 41.8 years. Median hospital stay was 6.0 days and median IMCU stay was 2.2 days. ICU admission was not required in 50.1% of encounters. Rapid response team activation occurred in 38 encounters (8.5%), the majority for escalating withdrawal management. Patient-directed discharge occurred in 41.4% of encounters.

Conclusions: An IMCU dexmedetomidine protocol deployed across seven monitored units at 2 hospitals offers a replicable framework for managing medetomidine withdrawal while potentially mitigating critical care capacity challenges. Identified opportunities include modification of titration and dosing strategies and further investment in addiction consult infrastructure.

item.title: Lancet: Strengthening health systems to prioritise, provide care, and prevent osteoarthritis: a roadmap for global health policy
item.description:
By 2050, almost 1 billion people are expected to live with osteoarthritis-a disabling musculoskeletal condition with currently no cure. Despite its burden and costs, osteoarthritis remains largely invisible in national and global health agendas, is poorly integrated within service models for other chronic health conditions, and is frequently perceived as inevitable with ageing and associated with limited therapeutic options. This context drives an osteoarthritis identity problem that fuels frustration among those living with the disease and health-care professionals, perpetuates stigma and inequities, undermines access to effective interventions, and crucially, deprioritises osteoarthritis in health policy. How can health systems be strengthened to mitigate the burden of disease and prioritise the prevention and control of osteoarthritis? We outline a co-created, globally relevant roadmap for health policy responses for osteoarthritis prevention and care that extend beyond the UN's Agenda 2030 targets. The intended audience for the roadmap includes health policy makers, health services managers, clinicians, and civil society organisations. The roadmap anchors to three strategic priorities underpinned by guiding principles of a life course approach, prioritising health equity, and ensuring that responses are affordable and sustainable across economies. Priority 1: recognise and respond to osteoarthritis with capacity building in national surveillance of burden, cost, and modifiable risk factors, and explicitly embedding musculoskeletal health within national and subnational health policies. Priority 2: scale up high-value, person-centred, equitable care for approximately 600 million people living with osteoarthritis. This priority requires reframing of societal narratives around osteoarthritis and reconfiguring service models to integrate osteoarthritis into primary and chronic disease care while also addressing social, environmental, and commercial determinants of musculoskeletal health. Priority 3: slow the osteoarthritis trajectory via primary and secondary prevention targeted at excess bodyweight and joint injury, enabled by cross-sectoral and cross-disease cooperation. These priorities are supported by accelerators requiring global collaboration, within and outside the osteoarthritis community.

item.title: Chest: Effectiveness of Continuous Automatic Endotracheal Cuff Pressure Monitoring in Preventing Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit: A Randomized Controlled Trial
item.description:
Background: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a major healthcare-associated infection in critically ill children, primarily driven by microaspiration around the endotracheal tube cuff.

Research question: Does continuous automatic cuff pressure monitoring (CACPM) reduce the incidence of VAP compared to intermittent manual cuff pressure monitoring (IMCPM) in critically ill pediatric patients requiring mechanical ventilation?

Study design and methods: In this open-label, randomized controlled superiority trial, pediatric patients requiring mechanical ventilation for ≥48 hours were randomly assigned (1:1) to either CACPM or IMCPM. The target cuff pressure was strictly maintained at 20-25 cmH2O. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients developing VAP within 28 days following intubation, evaluated in the intention to treat population. Secondary outcomes included time to VAP diagnosis and target pressure compliance. Statistical approaches included Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and multivariable Cox proportional hazard regression.

Results: Among 241 randomized patients, ITT analysis showed lower VAP with CACPM than IMCPM (13.3% vs 24.0%; risk difference, -10.6 percentage points; 95% CI, -20.3 to -0.8; P=0.034), with similar PP findings (15.0% vs 26.6%; P=0.044). ITT incidence density was 15.7 vs 27.1 per 1,000 ventilator-days (IRR, 1.73; 95% CI, 0.94-3.18; P=0.080). Unadjusted time-to-VAP was nonsignificant (HR, 1.80; 95% CI, 0.976-3.321; P=0.060), whereas adjusted Cox analysis narrowly indicated a higher VAP hazard with IMCPM (HR, 1.90; 95% CI, 1.024-3.510; P=0.042). Target-pressure compliance was higher with CACPM (P<0.001).

Interpretation: CACPM significantly reduces the proportion of critically ill pediatric patients developing VAP compared with IMCPM. This preventive effect appears directly linked to improved target pressure compliance, suggesting that automated regulation could be a valuable addition to pediatric VAP prevention strategies.

item.title: Lancet: Addressing threats to future global health-what is the right timeframe?
item.description:
Our decisions today can support or threaten future human health. Insofar as we protect the planet or invest in fruitful research on pandemic countermeasures, we promote future wellbeing and health, sometimes at the present generation's expense. As we warm the planet, accelerate antibiotic resistance, or consume finite natural resources, we might serve present-day wellbeing or health at the expense of future generations. To decide which such trade-offs are legitimate or advisable, we need to know how to balance the health interests of future generations against each other and against our own. Should concerns for future health be confined to the 21st century as per the stated mission of the Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health? If not, how far into the future should they extend, and why? Population ethics is a branch of ethics that considers future populations' wellbeing. This Review, a part of the Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health, applies general insights from population ethics to future populations' health, and shows why that application is more complex than meets the eye.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Trends in Ophthalmic Hospital Transfers and Consultations Across US Academic Centers
item.description:
Importance: Academic medical centers increasingly serve as a safety net for urgent and complex ophthalmic conditions, yet trends in the demand for hospital-based ophthalmic services remain poorly characterized.

Objective: To characterize multi-institutional trends in ophthalmology interhospital transfer requests and emergency department (ED) and inpatient ophthalmology consultation requests (hereafter, consultations) from other departments within the same hospital, such as emergency medicine or internal medicine, at multiple academic medical centers in the US.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective, longitudinal, cohort study involved 14 hospitals affiliated with 10 academic medical centers across multiple geographic regions in the US, representing large urban tertiary referral centers serving diverse catchment populations. Participants were patients for whom ED and inpatient interhospital transfers for ophthalmic care were requested and/or accepted, and patients who received inpatient or ED ophthalmic consultation at participating academic medical centers from 2013 through 2024.

Exposure: Participating institutions were required to be academic hospitals with resident participation in on-call coverage and to maintain hospital transfer or consultation data from at least 2017 onward, with the earliest beginning in 2013.

Main outcomes and measures: Trends in population-adjusted and hospital volume-adjusted rates of ophthalmology interhospital transfer requests and ED and inpatient ophthalmology consultations.

Results: A total of 32 131 ophthalmology transfer requests, 23 560 accepted transfers, and 139 356 ophthalmology consultations (83 581 ED and 44 472 inpatient) were recorded across participating hospitals. Transfer requests increased by an aggregate 0.66 (95% CI, 0.51-0.81) per 100 000 state residents per year and accepted transfers by 0.34 per 100 000 state residents per year (95% CI, 0.17-0.51). Among the 7 institutions with consultation data, consultations increased by an aggregate 3.01 per 100 000 state residents per year (95% CI, 2.33-3.69), comprising 2.06 per 100 000 per year for ED consultations (95% CI, 1.51-2.61) and 1.08 per 100 000 per year for inpatient consultations (95% CI, 0.87-1.30). All aggregate trends were significant (false-discovery rate-adjusted P < .001).

Conclusions: In this cohort study, ophthalmic interhospital transfer requests and inpatient and ED ophthalmology consultations increased substantially across academic medical centers over the study period. These trends suggest growing demand for hospital-based ophthalmic care and increasing strain on ophthalmology hospital coverage, with important implications for workforce sustainability and health system planning.

item.title: Am J Respir Crit Care Med: Rare Coding Variants in FOXF1 are Associated with Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: Most patients with nonheritable forms of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) lack identifiable pathogenic variants. Increasing evidence suggests that, in addition to high-impact predicted loss-of-function variants, rare missense coding variants may also contribute to disease pathogenesis.

Objectives: We identified ultra-rare missense variants in FOXF1 in two index cases with PAH. FOXF1 encodes a highly conserved transcription factor essential for lung vascular development. We sought to define the frequency of FOXF1 variants, characterize FOXF1 expression, and assess the functional relevance of FOXF1 alterations in PAH.

Methods: Three independent international PAH cohorts were analyzed for predicted deleterious FOXF1 variants. FOXF1 expression was evaluated using bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing and immunofluorescence. Bioinformatic and chromatin-profiling approaches were used to identify potential downstream transcriptional targets, followed by promoter-reporter assays in vitro.

Measurements and main results: Nine novel and one rare missense variants, one start-site variant, and one in-frame deletion in FOXF1 were identified across the three cohorts. FOXF1 expression was reduced in PAH lungs and localized predominantly to the endothelial cell compartment. Histopathological analysis revealed heterogeneous FOXF1 expression, with the lowest levels in phenotypically abnormal endothelial cells within complex vascular lesions. Single-cell analyses confirmed reduced endothelial FOXF1 expression in PAH, whereas broad FOXF1 downregulation across endothelial populations was not observed in other chronic lung diseases. Integration of CUT&Tag and ATAC-seq identified a canonical FOXF1-binding motif within the BMPR2 promoter. Promoter-reporter assays further supported FOXF1-dependent transcriptional regulation of BMPR2 and demonstrated reduced transcriptional activity of PAH-associated FOXF1 variants.

Conclusions: Large-scale genomic and transcriptomic analyses support an association between FOXF1 dysregulation and PAH and identify BMPR2 as a potential downstream transcriptional target.
